speechtext: So agreed. The hon. member for Edmonton Northwest.

Mr. Speaker, since I did not stay up all night preparing a speech for this morning, I will in the spirit of co-operation attempt to stay to around 10 minutes or so.
Today of course we are debating Bill C-28, the amendments to the Income Tax Act that flow from this year's budget presented by the Minister of Finance in April.
Before addressing the tax matters that are in this particular piece of legislation, one should consider the context in which they are being put forward, because in any budget there are a number of elements.
First, there is the presentation of the government's fiscal plans for the year including its spending plans. From that we can determine the government's financial requirements, and from that the government must determine how they are going to fund those financial requirements, either through borrowing, through taxation, or perhaps through some other means.
If we take a look at the last five years during which time this government has been governing, we have seen a fairly consistent pattern over that time. Government spending in the over-all has been held down to something less than the rate of inflation in the country. At the same time, the economy has grown, but there has also been some need to put in certain tax measures to fund essential programming.
When talking about the spending side we can look at four elements of government spending which are essentially where government money goes. The first element is interest. Unfortunately, we have a large accumulated debt which generates an annual interest bill each year of about $30 billion. That, of course, must be paid through the interest payments, Canada Savings Bonds and other means that the government uses to finance its debt and its borrowing. We have approximately $30 billion a year in interest payments.
The second element of government spending is transfer payments to provinces. That sounds complicated, but what it means is the money that we give to provincial governments to fund social programs in addition to then-own tax revenue. By far the largest element is the amount of money that goes to support health care at the provincial government level. It is approximately $25 billion. We can call that the second quarter or second element of government spending.
The third element is transfers to individuals which are essentially for pensions and family allowances, the vast bulk of which are for pensions.
When we look at those three elements of government spending we find that we have a very difficult time in trying to maintain spending or cut spending without diminishing those programs. First, in relation to interest, one would have to default on our bonds, default on our debt, or not pay Canada Savings Bonds. I do not think
October 17, 1989

anybody is suggesting that that would be a very proper thing to do.
The second element of government spending, the transfer payments to provinces to fund health care, most people believe that we should continue to pay. There is a formula under which the government pays that amount based on the growth in the economy each year which means that that bill continues to escalate.
First, we have the interest bill escalating by roughly $3 billion a year due to the continuing deficit, as long as that is there. Then we have the transfer payments to provinces increasing by an amount of about $1 billion a year simply to maintain our existing level of health care and other services. Then we have the third element, transfers to people, which are increasing every year because there are more and more people over the age of 65 in our population. Unless we can somehow stop people from ageing, we are going to have a continuing ageing population. That adds approximately $1 billion a year to the government's requirements.
With all of that, the government must find an additional $4 or $5 billion a year just to maintain those essential services. We often hear people saying that what they should really do is cut their expenditures. That is fine. I think that we would all like to do that. However, we must realize that any significant cuts in government expenditures are going to have to be addressed at those areas because when we come to the last quarter of government spending it goes for everything else. Now, that is the area in which most people want cuts, because they do not monitor it particularly carefully, it is somewhat diffuse, and there are a lot of civil servants out there who think that there is a lot of money available through waste and misuse to be found.
That last quarter of government spending goes to pay all the civil service salaries, offices for them to work in, paper for them to shuffle, and virtually all of the expenditures that go along with the operation and maintenance of the government, including police, customs agents, and for that matter, tax collectors, and I suppose some people think we could do with fewer of those.
Government Orders
That part of government spending has been held down. In fact, over the last five years it has been about 17 per cent of total government spending; it is about $1 billion less in absolute dollar terms than it was five years ago, in spite of the fact that we have had roughly 4 per cent inflation each year. The number of civil servants has been reduced to the 1972 level. That is the area that has borne the brunt of government expenditure cuts over the last five years, in order to support and maintain the other three areas that I described earlier. However, we have reached a point where we simply cannot make substantial cuts in that area any longer without seriously diminishing the services and the operations of the government which people desire.
We have two choices. We can either do something in the two areas, either through transfers to provinces which fund health care, or transfers to people which fund pensions, or we can try to increase taxation. This budget does some of both. In the area of transfers to people it is going to tax back and recover, from people with incomes of over $50,000 a year, the benefits that they received through the family allowance and pension system.
There have been some people who have been opposing this. There have been some people who have come to see me about this. I had a group of senior citizens come to see me about this. I told them what I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker.
In my view it is absolutely unfair for me to ask people who are in the workforce working or even trying to plan for their retirement, making an average income of $27,000 a year, which is approximately the average income in Canada, or perhaps living on an average family income of $47,000 a year, which is approximately the average family income in Canada, to pay more taxes so that we can continue to provide benefits to people who have retired, who are no longer in the workforce, who are over 65, and have substantially enough wealth that they still have an income of over $50,000 a year. We should not continue to pay them the old age security benefits. It would be totally unfair to tax people who are working, supporting families, trying perhaps to buy a home, trying to save a little for their retirement, earning $27,000 a year on average or $47,000 a year as a family, and ask them to pay more taxes so that we can continue

October 17, 1989
Government Orders
to pay benefits to people who are retired and over 65 and who have incomes of over $50,000 a year.
This measure taken by the Minister of Finance, while it is not supported by everyone and while it has not been supported so far by the opposition parties, is a measure of fairness. In order to continue to pay benefits to those people who are receiving pensions and maybe do not have other income or perhaps are receiving pensions and have an income of $10,000 or $12,000 a year, and there are many of these people in my riding, we are going to withdraw benefits from people with substantial incomes.
I am prepared to defend that in any forum. I have told people in my own riding that. I have told that to people who came to meet with me and I have written letters to that effect. We cannot continue to fund more and more benefits for more and more people without finding that money some place.
There was a tax rally in Edmonton a week or two back and it was ostensibly to protest the goods and services tax. The incredible thing that I found was that groups went there to have petitions signed at the same time they were protesting the paying of tax, which is another subject for another day. They were asking people to sign a petition to maintain the full benefits for people over 65, full pensions for people with incomes of over $50,000. I find it incredulous that on the one hand people can oppose paying taxes, then somehow suggest that we should find money from saving it through government expenditures, and then oppose what is essentially a benefit to people who do not need it.
I know that we agreed earlier to only talk for 10 minutes. While I would have liked to have gone on for 20 minutes, I will stop here. I wanted to cover that one point. I have many others I would like to address but I will have to save them for another day.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the member's speech. What does he think the proposal does to the principle of universality? Does it get away from "directions by indirections, fine", I think was Shakespeare's phrase. It has been explained to me that
people paying taxes between 1951 and 1972 paid premiums based on their taxable income.
Will the member tell the members of the House and perhaps Canadians at large whether he thinks it is fair to people who were obliged to pay premiums based on income and happened to have provided for their retirement by keeping the OAS as part of their retirement package? Why should they now be penalized, bearing in mind that these people pay taxes on the same basis as the rest of us do based on ability to pay. It is hardly getting a free ride when they say that they are entitled to OAS because it was used in retirement planning and when they are perfectly prepared to pay income tax based on their taxable income now.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to address some of those questions. First, the point was made that at one time, I believe up until about 1972, a special tax was designed or designated to fund old age security. That has not been there for many years now, at least 15 years. I would think that if we were to look at how much came in through that tax and look at the benefits that have been paid out since that time we would find that what came in has been paid out many, many times since then.
To suggest that money paid 15, 20, 25 years ago is still around to pay benefits is unrealistic. We can all talk about unfairness. There is a certain element of unfairness. I believe it is most unfair to ask people who are in the workforce earning $27,000 a year, perhaps supporting families, to pay additional taxes so we can fund benefits for people who are essentially in a position to not really require them.
If you have an income of $50,000 a year in retirement, you must have a substantial asset base. I just cannot believe for the life of me that we should somehow be suggesting that these people deserve more, but in order for them to have more, people who are earning $27,000 a year in the workforce, struggling to make a living, should be asked to pay more tax. It makes no sense to me.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate with the hon. member for Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt. Is the hon. member going to speak for 10 minutes?

Mr. Speaker, I will be taking the full 20 minutes.
October 17, 1989

It is a pleasure to rise today and speak on this bill. I should say right at the outset that since I was elected to Parliament in November of last year, I have had two occasions to rise and speak on bills in a positive vein. From the opposition point of view, that is something that comes too infrequently. Certainly it is a pleasure to be able to do it.
When we consider the present bill before us, historically I should be standing before you speaking positively on the expansion of the universality principle; on the expansion of benefits to our seniors and to our families with children.
On March 7, 1984, our Prime Minister said, "Our position is simple and straightforward. We are in favour of universality and social programs and it shall not be touched". Over the period of time there were attempts, particularly in 1985, perhaps not to touch the universality aspect, but certainly to de-index pensions of seniors. Of course, an outcry arose and, as a result of that outcry, the Prime Minister saw the folly of his idea and backed off.
On October 15, 1988, in Summerside, Prince Edward Island, Mr. Mulroney again approached our seniors and told them, "Let me say a special word to the senior citizens. In the future, Canada will be doing more not less for all of you. As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved not diminished by our government which is committed to social justice and fairness for Canadians".
Now arising out of that particular quote, again I fully expected to be able to come before Parliament and, as an opposition member, pat the government on the back for the expansion of its social programs, for its assistance to the elderly and for coming up with better programs such as daycare and such as a better family allowance assistance for the families of Canada who are struggling today.
When I examined Bill C-28, and the government's approach to the family and to the seniors aspect, I found that this government, that had promised to make things better for our seniors, was reneging on that promise. I would suggest that it is attacking the very principle of universality that has grown so near and dear to us in Canada.
Government Orders
This clawback does not maintain the principle of universality as Mr. Mulroney and Mr. Wilson have contended. It marks the steady erosion-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would hope that the hon. member would recognize these individuals by their portfolios. Thank you.

I do apologize for that, Mr. Speaker.
The principle of universality has not been maintained, as the Prime Minister and Minister of Finance have contended. It marks the steady erosion of our social programs, down to a much lower denominator. From now on social programs will be for the poor only. They will be targeted for those in need and, thereby, made selective, not universal. The clawback will move our pension system closer to that of the United States. No pension exists in the United States as a right of citizenship, but it does in Canada for those over the age of 65. This is something that we in Canada, our parents, our grandparents and those before, have worked hard for over a lengthy period of time. And now we have seen the wedge being driven in by this government.
It is interesting to note that in a letter to a person in Edmonton, the chairman of the finance committee said: "We have decided to eliminate universality. While a clawback may be unfair and sneaky, it is there". Well I suggest that this clawback is unfair and it is sneaky. In fact, it does through the back door what this government has promised not to do-attack the very basis of universality that we in Canada have grown to understand as a right.
We do not need and we do not want a system that is based on need, that is based on a means test. We are different in Canada and we are proud of it. Throughout history we have not been the same as our neighbours to the south.
If we in the opposition have anything to say about it, I suggest we will not be the same in spite of how hard this government tries to harmonize those of us who were born and raised in Canada and those of us who have immigrated here and set up homes. It will not be able to suppress that difference in Canadians. In spite of the fact that we now have the free trade agreement, and those pressures within that free trade agreement to harmonize many aspects of our Canadian life that we hold near and dear, we shall not give up or give in without a fight. I suggest that pressures will be so enormous against the

October 17, 1989
Government Orders
harmonization of our social programs with those of the United States, that this government will not be able to quiet the din that they will hear from all across Canada.
It is not just the goods and services tax that will hit our seniors and our families, it is methods such this clawback of old age security and family allowance that threatens the very principle that the basis of universality is built upon. We will hear the arguments in support of the clawback that is proposed in this bill, and have already heard some this morning, that those who make $50,000 a year really do not need the assistance of the old age security or the assistance of the family allowance. But what they fail to point out is that the system that has been set up, with a level now of $50,000, is the thin edge of the wedge. Any future government can drop that level to $40,000, to $30,000,or to $20,000, as it sees fit in order to break down our present system of pensions and family allowances. That is the crux of the argument. Once the door has been partially opened, it is but a small push to open it the rest of the way and create the flood toward the complete destruction of our social programs. We on this side of the House and in this comer of the House will not allow that to happen.
The other factor that we have to look at in this clawback is the fact that it is only partially indexed to the rate of inflation, so that up to 3 per cent is not taken into consideration from year to year.
At today's $50,000 level, as Mr. Wilson says, only approximately 4 per cent of Canadians are affected by the clawback. However, if we look at the facts, we know that within 10 years the number of seniors who will have at least part of their old age security clawed back will be one in twelve, or up 8 per cent from 128,000 to 300,000 persons. In 20 years, that number will be one in four, or one million people, or 25 per cent of those receiving it will now be giving at least part of it back. The amount will drop back so that eventually the average will drop.
Right now, if we look at family allowances, we know that the average Canadian income is $45,000. It does not take much imagination to see that within a year or two even those now making $45,000, with the rate of inflation going up at least 3 per cent, will be paying back at least part of what they get in family allowance. We have
effectively turned our system into that of a means test. If you need it, you get it.
Our contention is that these people are already paying tax. The unfairness of this clawback is readily apparent. Those with two incomes in a family, perhaps one at $45,000 and the other at $35,000-will be excluded. They will not have to pay any of it back. Yet one person making $56,300 will end up having to pay all of their family allowance back to the government. They pay their taxes which go into this assistance. Now they are going to have to pay back what they are getting as a credit toward having a family. It is unfair. It is discrimination against those with families. They are being doubly taxed.
Similarly, it has been pointed out many times by seniors, that since the 1950s and until 1972,1 believe up to 4 per cent of income was paid toward the old age security. In 1972 that was wrapped in and was not taken into account. I suggest that it is, in fact, part of the tax system and has continued to be paid since 1972. Many people point out that they have paid for their old age security. They have set their budgets accordingly and they have anticipated that income in calculating out their savings throughout that period. I would like to read to the House some comments and in one case almost a complete letter. A gentleman has written to me from Penticton, which is in my riding of Okanagan-Similka-meen-Merritt, and has asked if it would be possible to read his letter to the House of Commons. He states:
The old age pension is a pension. That is how it is defined now. It is not welfare. It is a form of wealth. It was not granted for need, as welfare is, but for merit to deserving people as pensions are.
The obvious objective of this government is to redefine that pension as welfare. They obviously hope to do that by taxing and treating it like welfare. Once that tax, and its new definition, has been accepted by Canadians the government can decrease it or eliminate it. They are already eliminating some people's old age pensions. Obviously they will not get much additional revenue from those few people so how safe are the pensions? This government obviously knows they may not be able to make this odious tax grab stick if it is challenged. No wonder they are spending millions of our tax dollars trying to trick Canadians into accepting their newly fabricated definition.
Obviously then Canadians should not let this government tax anyone's old age pension any differently than any other pension. United we stand, divided we fall. Canadians shouldn't be deceived. It is obviously only to reduce the sympathy and support, that other Canadians might give to the first victims of this odious scheme, that the government has put the amount of their current means test high
October 17, 1989

enough so that most pensioners will not be affected at this time. Who knows how much lower that amount will be in the future? Forty, thirty, twenty thousand or will the pension be abolished altogether? That seems most likely.
Cunningly these deceitful people are suggesting that other pensioners might get their own pensions increased from the funds extracted from their fellow pensioners. Is that likely? Can anyone believe that? These people have said they want to reduce the deficit. Are they not now actually cutting back on social programs? Are they likely then to increase anyone's old age pension? Can they be trusted? What is their record? Remember their actions, not their words? Do they deserve anyone's trust? Divide and conquer seems to be their dominant policy in relation to so many things.
Every person getting that pension now could lose it and there might well be no such pension in the future for any other deserving Canadians. No one's old age pension is safe.
Our government can obviously, even now if they choose, increase old age pensions without taking away anyone's pension. All they need do is to collect more taxes from all those people who are not now paying their fair share. Or they can raise the tax rate for all Canadians in the upper tax brackets. Or they can tax the excessive wealth that discriminatory tax policies make possible. How about the excessive wealth of the multi-millionaires and billionaires? Those people can't possibly earn such wealth can they? Do they need it?
It is signed by A. J. Lancey. That gives an idea of how people are viewing government and government policies. One of my constituents in East Gate, Manning Park, states in respect to what is happening:
I am writing you to express my deep concern over the finance minister's proposed shabby treatment of Canadians in their twilight years. I am referring of course to Mr. Wilson's proposed removal of universality of the old age pension through his scheme to grab it back through taxation.
It seems to me that when you contribute all your working life and in fact are obliged to contribute as in the case of old age security tax, that it takes a pretty damned dishonest as well as uncaring person, to seek to snatch away your well earned benefit just about the time you had every fair and reasonable right to start enjoying such benefit.

zation has said that: "The government is obviously ending universality but does not want to actually say those words". One Voice, a seniors group, has stated that: "Changes represent an erosion of universality and would unfairly target senior citizens". The Vanier Institute of the Family has said that: "The proposals effectively withdraw what little support remains for the family".
I will not be the only voice speaking from the wilderness. There are many of us across Canada who are telling this government that enough is enough. Leave our social programs alone.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a brief comment and ask my fellow member a question.
I would simply remind him that before I entered politics in 1984, I worked with families and with seniors and I very well know the difference between the principle of universality and the practice of it.
The measure presented by the Canadian Government is fair and equitable.
I met seniors throughout Canada in the last six months and I discovered full citizens who want to share and take part in the Canadian challenge that we are offering them as a Canadian Government.
The measure we are proposing therefore does respect the practice of universality, which for me means ensuring that every Candian who is 65 or over has at least a minimum. Name me just one Canadian (over 65) who does not get an old age security cheque! The very principle of the old age security pension is to provide needy persons with a minimum and as a responsible government, our responsibility is to help the less fortunate.
I would therefore like to ask my colleague to tell me how he can say to Canadians who are 65 or older that the measure we are advocating does not respect universality. We are asking those earning at least $50,000 net to show solidarity and I know that many Canadians I have met agree to take this challenge because together we must have some extra funds to improve our social programs, just to help the seniors who really need it.

October 17, 1989
Government Orders

I am somewhat surprised. I have a great deal of respect for the minister. I think that for the most part, she is an excellent minister. She has the best interests of seniors at heart.
However, having said that, I am somewhat surprised at the minister. She told the House that over the last six months she has spoken to various seniors groups, and perhaps they agree that we have to attack the problem of the deficit and deficit financing, but I do not think that any of those groups have said that they are in agreement, either partially or in principle, with this massive clawback, this unfair double taxation of what they, as seniors, have worked so hard to gain throughout their lives.
They do not mind paying their fair share and they are very clear on that, but they do not want to have to pay more than their share. They want others who are not paying their share, such as the large corporations, such as the wealthy, such as the high income earners with incomes over $80,000 a year, to pay their share. I suggest to the minister that they are now in their golden years, now in the years that they have looked forward to for travelling, enjoying themselves, relaxing and not having to worry about where their money is coming from. They do not feel that they should have to carry the burden of taxation in Canada.
I agree with them. I do not think that they should, after all of these years of working and assisting the government in bringing taxation into the coffers, have to do more than their fair share. Let us tax those with the ability to pay, as they have suggested. Let us not attack the family. Let us not grab from the seniors when they are least able to defend themselves because I, for one, will stand in my corner and I will kick and I will fight and I will stand up for the rights of those seniors if they cannot do it themselves.

Mr. Speaker, one of the proudest heritages of this country is the fact that we are, indeed, a compassionate and tolerant society. I am very proud to stand up on this side of the House and say that that is the heritage of the Liberal party to this country.
I would like to congratulate the member for his speech and for his very clear enunciation of policies which we in the Liberal party have created since the Second World War. I would like to welcome him in this broad Liberal philosophy that we have created, this philosophy of
understanding the needs of the poor and the disadvantaged and the downtrodden.
My question to the member is, could he possibly explain to this House how it is that the Conservative Party has a philosophy which is so alien to that which is held by the vast majority of Canadians? Does he understand why the Conservative Party and this government are prepared to claw back from senior citizens money which they have paid into the government's funding in order to maintain a decent and universal system of pensions in this country?
Does the member feel that the government adequately consulted with seniors in this country before expropriating their savings? I would like to ask the member if he could possibly explain to us how it is that we have elected a government which is so foreign to the needs and the aspirations of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for his questions. I would like to point out that the social programs that we have seen developed in Canada are the legacy of the likes of M. J. Coldwell, J. S. Woodsworth, Tommy Douglas, David Lewis and Edward Broadbent. We in this party are very proud of those former leaders and the fact that they were able to show the government in power at that time the error of its ways and the ways of the future. We thank them very much for seeing that and for bringing in the legislation that has been near and dear to and a basis of our party for so long.
To turn to. the hon. member's question with respect to the government, I often wonder how a government that speaks and talks as if it is caring can then trip the very people that it says it is caring about and tramp them into the mud as it stomps by them. It is truly a shocking policy of an uncaring government.
We have worked so long in the past to try to make equal some of those within our society, and now under the free trade agreement with its various pressures for harmonization, all of the things that have been worked toward since the Second World War in particular, and since the turn of the century with the advent in the early 1900s of some of our old age security systems, are being eroded because of an uncaring government.
I think that we on this side of the House must ensure that the people of Canada well recognize that there is more on the plate of this government for them in the future. We must stand up and ensure that measures that will hurt the poor, measures that will hurt those on fixed incomes, measures that will hurt the family and mea-
October 17, 1989

sures that will hurt seniors will be stopped and blocked now.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I would agree to talk for ten minutes and after to have five minutes of questions to permit others of my colleagues to also have time to participate in this debate.
Also I will talk about Bill C-28, the income tax review. [Translation]
In fact, about the Income Tax Act and related legislation. Mr. Speaker, I think it is important that taxpayers, that all Canadians be aware of the major aspects of this Bill. In fact, the measures contained in this enabling legislation reflect the commitment made by the Government to reduce the deficit and improve the fairness of our tax system. These measures include a high-income surtax; second, a deduction in respect of part-time attendant care expenses for the working disabled; third, the refundable sales tax credit will be doubled and the income threshold at which the credit starts to be reduced will be increased; furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the new tax on large corporations and modifications to the existing corporate surtax are expected to raise an additional one billion dollars from the corporate sector in the first full year of application of these measures.
Mr. Speaker, those were a few highlights, but the 1989 budget's measures are in line with the objectives of the 1987 income tax reform, and they support-in fact they will provide for a more stable tax base which will help the government deal more efffectively with the deficit. They also help create an investment climate that is a response to economic rather than fiscal considerations. Finally, and most important, Mr. Speaker, they improve the fairness of our tax system by requiring high-income Canadians and the corporate sector to contribute to a greater extent to meeting the government's revenue requirements.
Mr. Speaker, when we talk about raising taxes and reducing the deficit, it is always difficult to explain to taxpayers that they must contribute more to the economy of their country. However, the government's perspective- On the weekend in Jonquiere, the riding whose residents I have the honour to represent in this House, I
Government Orders
was telling taxpayers that our government was even better than it was in 1984.1 explained that in 1984, many of our Tory members had been elected for the very first time. We did not have much experience but we were ready and willing, and we really wanted to help improve the situation in this country and reduce the debt so that we could maintain social programs. Gradually, however, because of our lack of experience and at a time when we might have been able to introduce new legislation and apply new measures, we had to cope with a series of political scandals, which was a very trying time for all members in this House.
The government has now been given a second mandate. It has a very solid agenda, Mr. Speaker, and we now have a chance to implement decisions which had been postponed or delayed. Now we have to do something. We have no choice. The debt is now 324 billion dollars and costs us between 80 and 100 million dollars a day in interest. One hundred million dollars a day! In the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region, when we talk about what it costs to build a highway from the Saguenay to Quebec City, we are talking about $200 to $300 million. With two or three days' worth of interest payments, we could build a highway so that the Saguenay would have far more convenient and safer access to the Quebec City area, for instance. Unfortunately, we cannot pick up those two or three days' worth of interest payments and take them home. The government can't do that, and meanwhile, the whole region may have to wait ten, twenty or thirty years for that highway.
One hundred million dollars a day in interest payments, Mr. Speaker-You know what our social programs cost, including old age security pensions and family allowances. If we didn't have to pay $100 million a day in interest on our debt, we could give a lot more to the taxpayer. One hundred million a day in interest payments, Mr. Speaker, is as if every day, the government sent a cheque for $20,000 to 5,000 people. Do you realize how many people we could pay this kind of salary in one year? That is what our debt costs us every day.
Mr. Speaker, we must understand that when we want to reduce a debt-Remember that in 1984, when we came to power, the debt was $200 billion. Five or six years- later, the debt has now increased to $324 billion. Canadians may not realize this but when we came to

October 17, 1989
Government Orders
power, the government's annual deficit was $38 billion. So when we were elected, with this $200 billion debt plus the annual deficit, we were in for $238 billion. The following year, we were able to reduce the deficit from $238 billion to $234 billion, but $34 billion was still added to the deficit, and the process goes on. Now we have managed to keep our annual deficit down to about 28 or 30 billion dollars, but it keeps adding up.
And that is why the government can no longer afford to provide these social programs, unless it takes certain steps that are necessary.
I think that event if my colleagues in the NDP and the Liberal party, are against tax increases, they will understand that, as a responsible government, we have to act, we have to do what is necessary, because otherwise we would be acting irresponsibly towards future generations of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I saw the same thing when I was a member of the Legislative Committee on Bill C-21. I travelled across this country for three weeks. We visited all 10 provinces of this country. I saw provinces with an unemployment rate that was lower than average, and I saw others with an unemployment rate that was higher. In British Columbia, I saw a very prosperous city, Vancouver, a delightful place. However, I saw other parts of Canada like Newfoundland which is not as well off as the other provinces. I met people in St. John's. The economic situation is different.
With a vast country like ours, the government has to try and reduce regional disparity and get the richer provinces to pay for the poorer provinces, so that everybody will be happy in this beautiful country of ours and we can have social programs for all Canadians.
Still on the subject of unemployment insurance reform, and I think this is an important point, about 200 different groups appeared before our committee with briefs in which they explained their views. Across this country, people were saying: "Sure, we agree with your plan to do more through unemployment insurance reform, but not with what you want to remove, what you want to remedy. If you want to use $800 million to train workers, when 30 per cent of our young people drop out before they even finish high school, if you want to spend
$800 million more on training, that's fine. But don't take the money from the unemployment insurance fund. Thke it out of taxes. Get more money from the taxpayers. Unfortunately, we can no longer afford to do that, either as a government or as Canadians.
We now have to take the money we have to reallocate. Let me give you an example, Mr. Speaker. Let us assume we have 989 different programs in this country. There may be 1,000 or 1,050 but let us say there are 989 different programs. If every time we want to give Canadians a little more, we have to add one more program, there comes a time when we have to ask the question: Where is the money going to come from?
That is the problem. We have to look at these programs and cancel the ones that are no longer effective or not as good as they were, and then take the money and reallocate it to better programs that will meet the needs of Canadians, that respond to the present situation and reflect the Government's new perspective and the new needs of Canadians.
So that was an example of using new funds. Remember what the Liberals said when we cut the Katimavik program. We even had Senator Hebert on a hunger strike in front of the Senate Chamber! He said it didn't make sense to cut the program, that we were doing a terrible job as a Government. However, nobody even talks about the program anymore, and I think everybody will agree we were right to do what we did. We saved money and we took that money and spent it or- other programs.
Mr. Speaker, the legislation before the House today reflects the government's policy of trying to maintain the standard of living and quality of life of Canadians and ensure we can keep our social programs. We have to bear this in mind, Mr. Speaker. We have no choice. This is serious stuff! We have this debt and there are no two ways about it.
I want to ask all members of this House to work together so that this bill can be referred as soon as possible to committee, so the government can proceed with the other items on its agenda.
I think unemployment insurance reform Bill C-21, will be particularly important.

I also believe that the goods and services tax, and I will talk about that later because I have a lot to say about it- If my collegues have any questions, I will be glad to try answer them.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his speech. I have a question for him. He indicated in his opening remarks that he would like to address the bill so that perhaps Canadians could understand it. I have a copy of the bill in my hand which contains some 84 pages and which proposes to amend a number of different acts. I would like to ask my colleague basically about integrity.
In 1987 the Minister of Finance indicated that the surtax which had been brought in would be removed when a new sales tax was introduced. We know that there is going to be a new sales tax introduced. That is what we have been talking about for the last little while. Lo and behold, if we look at Bill C-28, and I direct my hon. friend specifically to clause 47 of that bill, we see that Section 180.1 of the Income Tax Act is going to be amended, not in fact to remove the surtax but rather- and I wonder how many Canadians really know or appreciate this-to increase it from 3 per cent to 5 per cent across the board, and in addition, to increase it a further 3 per cent for those people who pay over $15,000 in tax in a taxation year, bringing it to 8 per cent.
I would ask my colleague to comment first on the fact that his own Minister of Finance indicated on June 18, 1987 that when the new sales tax was brought in the surtaxes would be removed, and why we have in Bill C-28 not only a failure to remove surtaxes but an increase of those surtaxes. This on top of the sales tax that this callous government is expecting Canadians to pay.

Mr. Speaker, I understand my colleague is trying to find something in the Bill whereby the government will get more money.
However, my colleague forgets to mention the good points for many Canadians.
I see my colleague smile. He does not seem to find any in the bill! What about the tax credit we have almost doubled, Mr. Speaker! I think that is a very positive measure that our government is presenting just so low-income Canadians can have more money and be
Government Orders
able to handle the various cost-of-living and other increases in this country. We propose to do the same thing with the future goods and services tax! Let us remember, and I remind my colleague, that the new 9 per cent tax will replace the old 13.5 per cent tax that is now applied to nearly 75,000 manufacturers. There are about 22,000 different regulations and interpretations to collect the 13.5 per cent tax. We will do away with that and replace it with a new 9 per cent tax.
So that low-income Canadians can absorb this 9 per cent tax, we will send them four cheques a year to compensate for it. For a family with two children, for example, that amounts to about $715. For a single person, it is over $400. That is an example of the tax credit that we will give to low-income individuals to help them with this new tax.
The same thing is in this bill: the sales tax credit is being raised to help give taxpayers the income they need to deal with difficulties and meet their obligations and buy things as they like.
I think that Canadians-I can tell you, I met people from Revenu budgetaire who do tax returns. This is a voluntary organization in my riding that helps low-income taxpayers get the famous sales tax credit and the other amounts the government gives every year to those whose income is under $15,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I ask whether we are going to have the pleasure of a 20-minute speech or a 10-minute speech from the hon. member for Burin-St. George's?

Mr. Speaker, I believe I can say what I want to say in 10 minutes. That might come as a surprise to you, Sir, but I will do my very best.
I suppose it is appropriate that the last two Tories who spoke scattered from the chamber very quickly, particularly the gentleman from Jonquiere who puts on a very brave front. He is probably still within the hearing of my voice and I want to say to him before he disappears altogether that I admire him for his ability to put on a brave front. I caution him, however, that he ought not to carry that too far because nobody is believing the Tory line on this issue. This Bill C-28 is a disaster from the word go, and the less he talks for the record, the better

October 17, 1989
Government Orders
for him down the road, assuming he has a place down the road.
I want to come just for a moment, to the gentleman from Edmonton Northwest because I found what he had to say to be among the more interesting, if incredible things, said in this debate thus far. I watched him single-handedly bear that public debt for all of Canada and my heart went out to him, that this young man, as virile as he is, should have to carry alone that load of many millions and billions of dollars, carrying it all by himself.
I would like to ask him where he was last November when his Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance were out campaigning, completely ignoring any possibility that there might be a debt load or that it might be crippling the country as we are now being told and, instead, were promising all kinds of things in the billions of dollars. When they were confronted with the possibility that maybe this would cost a few dollars or this might only be election time promises which would be forgotten after, we remember the immortal words of the gentleman who was the Minister of Finance: "These are not even promises, these are spending commitments. We are going to do these because it is within our budgetary framework and our fiscal ability to do them".
That was in November. Now it is the following October. It is hardly a year since and what are we told now? We are told that this nation is grinding to a halt because of the debt. Well, which is it? Is it in good shape as he told us last November, or do we have to attack seniors and families now to claw back every last cent we can to save us from grinding to a halt completely as a country? Which is it? Is it the story we were told last November that everything was hunky-dory or is it the story we are being told now by the gentleman from Edmonton Northwest, he who carried single-handedly that great debt on his own very shoulders this morning?
If they want to be able to meet their spending commitments, as the minister characterized them last fall, if they want to find a few shekels to better finance the public debt, let them do something that is completely within their power, without attacking the widows and the seniors of this country, without clawing back money that
people have come to regard as part of their entitlement right back to the 1970s, as the other gentleman from Edmonton Southeast so rightly pointed out just now.
People in the 1970s made certain investments and they ought to be able to count on the return on those investments now in 1989 and years down the road. My point a moment ago was this, if they want to find a few shekels to better finance the public debt, let them do something that is within their power to do. Let them lower the interest rate one-half point or a point. Why is it that in every other matter, we have to be cheek by jowl with the Americans, but on the matter of interest rates, we have to be four points ahead of them?
If they want to ease the public debt situation, the ability to meet payments, they can cut down the payments substantially by lowering the interest rate. They would, in the process, not only eliminate a lot of pain for the government but for a lot of people who are suffering under this high interest rate inflicted by this government or aided and abetted by this government at the very least.
Now the gentleman from Edmonton Northwest also talked about fairness. In courtesy to him, I did not completely laugh out loud, but when he talks about this issue in terms of fairness, he might as well also try and tell us, yes, that Dracula is really a nice fellow.
Old age security is now a fair system. Anybody who tampers with it, as this bill would do, cannot in the same mouthful pretend that he is doing it in the interest of fairness. There is nothing fair about this exercise whatsoever.
This claw-back of family allowance and pensions-we should see it for what it is-is simply and despicably a foot in the door approach. This is just the beginning. Seniors realize this and that is why we are beginning to hear from them again on this particular issue. They saved the issue the first time around when the Prime Minister went back on his now famous sacred trust commitment. In 1985 he tried to go back on it and the seniors saved it. I am depending on them again to save it this time.
They are already mobilizing the so-called grey power out there. They are mobilizing, bless their hearts, and they are going to save the day for us on this one because they see it for what it is. It is not just a claw-back on

incomes of $50,000 and over, no, it is more than that. It is the foot in the door.
What guarantee do they have, they ask me as I travel around this country, that the $50,000 will not be $45,000 and then will not be $40,000 in another year. Of course, with inflation and the ever increasing cost of living, $50,000, even if it were frozen there, will not be worth quite what it is now a few years down the road.
What guarantee do my people in Belleoram, Beaubois and Barachois Brook have that the $50,000 will not be $40,000? I am delighted to mention Belleoram because I see right in front of me the gentleman from Labrador who had the good sense to be born in Belleoram.
Why then are the Tories doing this? Why this bill at all, why the claw-back? What is this all about? I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that like almost everything we are seeing in the House these days, whether it is VIA Rail or the sabotaging of job creation programs or the UI changes or the GST or the ruling yesterday on the west coast fishery, it is all part of the same right wing agenda, it is all part of the same kotowing strategy with the Americans.
Do not forget that the Prime Minister's curriculum vitae basically is that of being a branch plant manager for an American multinational. He really never stopped being that when he became the Prime Minister. Instead, he just set about making the country a branch plant operation. We see it here, as insidious as it is, it is here too.
He is aware, and it has been pointed out to him many times, that our social programs, medicare, family allowance and old age security net are much more adequate here than in the United States. The senior who lives in Michigan has not the same support system as the senior in Manitoba. The senior who lives in New Hampshire has not the same support system from the public purse as does the senior who lives in Newfoundland.
It is all part of the old level field commitment that the Prime Minister made to the Americans. "Give me time", he said in effect, "Give me time and I will beat my crowd down to your level. My medicare, my pension, my family allowance will be as measly as yours if you give me time to work on it". This bill is just the latest cowardly
Government Orders
manifestation of that gentleman's agenda, an agenda that will reduce us to a branch plant, a shadow, if you like, of what is happening in the United States.
There are a thousand other reasons which I will not go into because I gave the Chair a commitment that I would finish in 10 minutes to allow some others to speak. I thank you, Sir, for your indulgence. I feel strongly about this issue and I urge my colleagues to vote against it for the sake of the seniors across the country.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague for another display of great oratorical skills for which he has become famous. I have a simple question. I know there is no point in presenting this to members opposite; I would not get the answer.
This new tax was supposed to be up front. To me a primary way of having something up front would be having it visible on the sales slip. I understand this will not be on the sales slip. It is hard to believe that every speech we have heard this morning from the opposite side of the House seems to suggest that this is going to be implemented to reduce the deficit. It was supposed to be revenue neutral, but now it is obvious that that cause has been abandoned. It was supposed to be simple, but I can tell you, Sir, that any small businessman is going to be driven completely around the bend on this one.
I wonder if my colleague would care to comment on those three basic, simple rules which were supposed to be held in place but have been totally abandoned.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for Leeds-Grenville. He is so right, of course. Whether we are talking about the clawback on pensions and family allowance or about the goods and services tax, we can see the same pattern. The pattern is one of smoke and mirrors. It is one of we will say we are doing this, while we are really doing that-we will say to pensioners in 1984 that we would never, never tamper with old age pensions and then in the spring of 1985 we will go out and try to do it; we will say to the voters in the fall of 1988 that if we ever have a goods and services tax, I assure you it will be revenue neutral and it will be visible on the sales slip. Then a few months later when push comes to shove, when it comes time to get the

October 17, 1989
Government Orders
legislation before the House, all the talk of visibility is gone, all the talk of being revenue neutral is gone.
We will say to voters when we are looking for their votes in 1984 that we will not only protect and preserve VIA Rail, we will enhance it; but when it comes to the crunch in 1989 of course we will do the exact opposite.
The Prime Minister will say here in the House that we are fighting to save VIA Rail. When we get to Hong Kong we will have a slip of the tongue and we will tell the truth, say we are getting rid of VIA Rail back in Canada. We will say to people in 1984 on the television debate: "Is not patronage awfully shocking?" Then, we will get aboard the plane with the press boys and let our hair down and say: "I would do the same thing if I were there at the time".
That is what we are dealing with-unabashed, bare faced hypocrisy. We cannot believe a word the Prime Minister tells us. We cannot believe a word the Minister of Finance tells us on THIS issue, and that is what makes this bill on clawback so frightening. Even as dastardly as this reality is, we never know if this is only half the punch we are going to get because we never know what this crowd is going to come up with next.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Then I will have to recognize the hon. member for Nepean, and following her I will recognize the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam.

Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful for the chance to rise today and speak on Bill C-28, an act to amend the Income Tax Act and the Old Age Security Act. There are 59 different amendments to the Income Tkx Act and I could not possibly discuss them in the time allotted. Hence, I will confine my comments to the way in which this government has dealt with the senior citizens of this country.
The clawback proposal puts a special tax on our senior citizens, a tax that does not apply to anyone else in this
country. In this way the clawback is anti-senior. I am one who feels that the senior citizens in our country deserve our utmost respect. This government's proposed clawback are the ultimate signs of disrespect.
Beginning in the fiscal year 1990-91 the government will effectively end universality of social benefits in Canada. People who bought and paid for old age securities in the years before 1971 were assured by the House of Commons in debate, when tax reform went through in 1971, that they would continue to be entitled to old age security.
Income Security for Canadians, a document put out in 1970 by the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Hon. John Munro, promised seniors in this country that any payments they were to make into old age security were theirs.
Today we are hearing that in a couple of years from now no longer will those same seniors be allowed to keep the money that they paid in so that they could look after themselves in their old age. Now these same senior citizens are finding that rather than the government looking after them they have to look after the government. This is an absolutely disgraceful situation.
In 1984 the Prime Minister said that social programs were a sacred trust, never to be tampered with. Well, he lied. And those same seniors told him he lied, right here on Parliament Hill. I say that we Canadians are beginning to realize just how loose the government is with the word "trust". We Canadians are beginning to realize just how little we can trust this government.
This government's proposed clawback of old age security is just one example of many showing how this government does not have the best interests of Canadians at heart.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member to repeat. Did the hon. member say that the Prime Minister lied? Did she indicate that in her speech? If she did then she knows what she must do.

I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, I will withdraw the comment. The proposed clawback will tax the benefits of old age pensions at a rate of 15 per cent of an individual's net income over $50,000, rising to 100 per cent for incomes reaching $76,000. The government says that this will affect only 4.3 per cent of seniors.
October 17, 1989

As I pointed out in the Nepean Clarion, this is but the tip of the iceberg. Because the $50,000 threshold is to rise at a rate of 3 per cent less than inflation, clawback will start at $36,000 by the year 2000, and in 20 years it will start at $28,000 and affect 2 million Canadians.
These same Canadians were the ones who did without in their early years when their children were small. They did not take the trip to the southern climate. They did not buy the new car. They put that money away. These were ordinary people on an average income who were saving for the day when they could take that holiday or purchase that new car, and now that money has to be given back to the government. It is their money.
In an August 1989 article in The Voice, a bulletin by the Canadian Seniors Network, the whole concept of the clawback is summed up perfectly. The article reads:
The finance minister argues that since everyone receives a cheque
the program is still universal, but if you give someone a cheque and
take it back a year later that is no more than a short-term loan.
How right they are; a short-term loan. What a disgusting sign of respect for our seniors. Unfortunately the government has refused to take into consideration the recommendations made by the people, and as far as the government is concerned the people do not matter.
Senior citizens in this country have played an integral part in the building of this nation. They have toiled to make Canada the greatest nation on earth. Yet, what does our present government do to show its appreciation? It strips those same senior citizens of everything they have worked for. This government has spit in the collective face of our senior citizen population.
Last year during the election the Prime Minister of this country made repeated promises to keep these benefits for the elderly when he said: "As long as I am the Prime Minister of Canada social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved, not diminished by our government." The Prime Minister of this country made that statement.
I suppose the Prime Minister thinks that clawing back money from our seniors is an improvement in their welfare. What other kinds of mixed up ideas is this government going to introduce? It slashes VIA Rail by 51 per cent and claims to be saving it. It proposes a tax
Government Orders
that is supposedly revenue neutral, yet it will raise $24 billion in 1991. Scary proposals.
The clawback to the seniors of this country strikes a severe blow to the programs. It cuts at the quick of Canadian universality, the universality that has been a unifying force in our country, a country that prides herself in being the most successful in the world in taking care of her citizens.
This government has been undermining that approach. It has increased the gap between the haves and the have nots, between the young and the old. It is imperative that this government listen to Canadian citizens and eliminate the clawback.
I would like to quote from Robert Choquette of the French Canadian Academy. I think that he put it extremely well when he wrote:
It excites me when I think of millions of men and women-different from me and different from one another in origin, language, culture, history and tradition-who, too, think of Canada as their country. And I love the thought that everyone, or almost everyone, has always wanted her to be greater still, more beautiful, more confident of herself and her destiny. Those who discovered Canada felt that way. So did those who came later and toiled to develop the broad expanse waiting for plough and people. So did those who continue to arrive on her shores-because they have faith in her, because for them and for their children, Canada represents security and freedom and is the best answer to their hopes.
We must strengthen that security, not diminish it as this government and this bill are attempting to do.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to open my remarks by suggesting that the hon. member for LaSalle-Emard and the other hon. members in this room might like to talk to Stanley Knowles about the struggle and the fight for pensions in this country. They should think about the history of pensions in this country and they should think about why we have universality in this country. These are all major improvements. Universality in this country took place only after a minority government was forced by New Democrats to introduce it.
I would like to think about the year 1926 when Mackenzie King introduced a pension plan, $20 a month with a means test. If a senior had any savings at all, no pension. I would suggest that the Tory government today is following in that Liberal tradition and moving us back to the means test, back to the kind of pension that you get if you happen to meet a means test. I think hon. members in this room have expressed their respect for

Government Orders
Stanley Knowles and those who went before him by naming him, after 40 years of dedicated service and a sustained fight for good pensions in this country, an honorary officer of the Chamber with a seat at the table.
This legislation flies in the face of that parliamentary struggle, that parliamentary tradition, for which Stanley Knowles stands. This legislation with a claw in the door is a clawback on universality not only in pensions but in family allowances. The hon. Minister of State for Employment and Immigration and Minister of State for Seniors, in the question and comment period, talked about talking to seniors' groups which agree with this legislation. Yet when I challenged that statement last spring and asked the minister to name one, she was unable to do so.
I named in a statement in this House a long list of seniors' groups which oppose this clawback, and I would hope that before this legislation is indeed passed into law, sadly, that the hon. Minister of State for Employment and Immigration and Minister of State for Seniors could give us a list of the seniors groups which indeed support this legislation.
Last spring when this budget was introduced I was so alarmed by what the inference of the clawbacks was that I asked the Minister of Finance to explain to us whether he believed that, while 4 per cent of people have their pensions clawed back today, it is acceptable that in 20 years 25 per cent of people will have their pensions clawed back. His response was that the government would be reviewing the situation and that "we are acting when it is appropriate".
I would suggest that today, based on this legislation, we are indeed reviewing pension programs. In this instance the review is a backward step, a nasty step, a grabby step, and a step that should put all seniors in this country on their guard that their pensions will be continually eroded.
I asked the Minister of Finance, if we are talking about a vague review, how do we as Canadians know which way he is going to review it? The clawback that is being proposed is like quicksand into which more and more elderly Canadians are about to sink.
My question was: Is it acceptable to the minister that in 20 years one in four Canadians would be caught in that quicksand? His response was: "No, it is not acceptable". Yet the projection based on this legislation is that it is what we will be facing 20 years hence.
The hon. member from Edmonton Northwest said during the question and comments that obviously having a $50,000 a year income meant that one was operating with a substantial tax base and a substantial income base. Yes, indeed it does today, but the projections again show that by tomorrow-tomorrow meaning 20 to 25 years from now-we will be faced with over a million Canadians who are eligible today for old age pensions, who would not be eligible under this proposal.
I was so concerned about this-not only from the point of view that over a million Canadians would be faced with this in 20 years but also from the point of view of a two tier system or a breach of the universality to which Canada is committed-that I went to the Library of Parliament and asked if indeed under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms this piece of legislation would be acceptable.
The letter I received back from the Library of Parliament quoted subsection 15(1) of the Charter which reads:
Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental and physical disability.
The letter that I received back went on to say:
It is possible to argue that a separate system of taxation for Canadians aged 65 and over is discrimination based on age as one segment of the population would be treated differently from the rest, solely on the basis of age. However, there is an argument to be made that even if such a system is discriminatory it is justified.
I would expect that the government based on the legislation it has introduced would be trying to argue that this is justified under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Many Canadians and I believe that the Charter is very, very clear and very explicit on this point.
Proponents of the budget could argue that the purpose of old age security payments is to assist lower income Canadians. The whole basis on which our Canadian pension system is based is that it is there for all Canadians when they reach a certain age. It has nothing

to do with what their income is. With a progressive tax system, those who earn enough would be paying their fair share of taxes in an equitable way and those who are not would receive the full benefit of the pension.
Many of the speakers today have referred to the comments by the chairman of the finance committee about seniors. He said that they live at a slower pace and they do not spend money in the same sense that you and I do. Well, I guess if you do not have as much money as Members of Parliament have, you do not spend as much. He said that older people do not wear out their clothes. Is there some magic fabric that older people have in their clothes so that the clothes do not wear out? He said they do not wear out their furniture. Do older people have some kind of levitation that they do not actually sit on the furniture when they are sitting down, Mr. Speaker? Of course older people wear out their clothes, of course their furniture wears out. The difference is that older people do not have the disposable incomes that you and I have to replace those things so they do not spend as much money. I think it is absolutely shameful that a Member of Parliament should flaunt his good fortune at the expense of the seniors in our country, belittle them and suggest that their needs are not as great because they have achieved a certain age.
The Tory government knows that seniors, because of the very fact that their incomes are less, do not have the means to fight back. However, they have the network and they put that network together in 1984. But, Mr. Speaker, it is hardly fair that the seniors in this country should have to fight the same fight every four years. I would suggest that the government ought to rethink its introduction of this legislation and rethink the kinds of commitments it has made during election periods to the seniors of this country.
I would like to talk for a couple of minutes about how the clawback is really going to work. A worker earning $40,000 a year today and watching his or her income rise with inflation would be earning enough by the time he or she retired to be caught in the clawback for both pensions and family allowance.
Government Orders
For retirees the clawback is more complex, it phases in more slowly,, but a simple rule of thumb is that a worker who earns at his or her age, say a 28 year old worker earning $28,000 or the average industrial wage, will be hit by the clawback by the time he or she retires. This assumes that incomes keep pace with inflation and that retirement income is 70 per cent of pre-retirement income.
If the government is successful, through the free trade deal and other economic factors in keeping workers' wages well behind inflation, then I would suggest that possibly as many pensioners as I am predicting will not be caught in the clawback. But that may suggest yet another piece of the over-all agenda of this government when it comes to working people, retired people, women and children and, in particular, those who are disadvantaged.
The implication is that the clawback of these social benefits will hit average income earners, not just the rich, in a very few years. Average Canadians will lose the benefits of the social programs that make us distinct from the U.S. More and more of our social programs will become poorer and poorer and more targeted and available only to those considered to be in need.
I suggest it is a very, very clever strategy on the part of this government to introduce this legislation by going after those who earn $50,000 or more. Of course we all say people who earn $50,000 or more should be paying taxes. But what the government does not say is how that projects, and who is next, and who is next and who is next. I would suggest that it is the same kind of philosophy that introduces amendments to the unemployment insurance bill, the inference of which is that we must change this, we must get those lazy people to work one or two more weeks before they go on to this program, and that most workers indeed somehow fiddle the system.
It is very clever strategy. It is strategy designed to bring out the worst in all of us, to bring out that in us which says, "I am working hard, why is he or she not?", without ever putting ourselves into his or her boots. I would suggest that these clawbacks on the pensions and the family allowance indeed are indicative of the kinds of over-all policy which the government has.

October 17, 1989
On family allowances, the proportion of families affected by the clawback will be more than double in 10 years. On old age security, the Minister of Finance likes to point out that his clawback will affect only 4 per cent of seniors. I repeat that in 10 years the number of pensioners seeing at least part of their old age pension clawed back will be one in 12, or 30,000, and in 20 years it will be one in four, or one million pensioners.
I think there are some fundamental questions that must be asked about this legislation which Canadians will be asking. They will be asking, why should an individual be entitled to receive $100,000 in capital gains, tax free, but lose the $4,000 he or she gets in old age security simply because it was paid as a universal social benefit? About family allowances and old age security, Canadians will be asking why the government is introducing a new tax when they are already taxed. Why should a special tax be levied on children and on the elderly?
They are vulnerable.

They are vulnerable. That is exactly why.
Canadians will be asking if the intention is to raise money from the rich, why not do it through a more progressive tax system instead of a super tax on children and a super tax on seniors? Why not raise marginal rates at the top to 32 per cent instead of taxing back family allowance and old age security?
Canadians will be asking what will the unique identity of Canada be in a few years when our social programs exist to serve only those in need? Will our social programs not be just like those in the U.S.-leaner and meaner, as all means-tested programs are?
Canadians will be asking how long will the population support the maintenance of social programs from which they are effectively excluded as beneficiaries? Canadians will also be asking will need be redefined downwards as it has been in Britain and in the U.S. and as it has already been with our UI program and other welfare programs?
Many hon. members before me have quoted the Prime Minister's comments on CP wire on March 7 when he said: "Our position is simple and straightforward. We are in favour of universality in social programs and it shall not be touched". Another remark, almost equally as famous, made on October 15 in Summerside, P.E.I., was
"As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved, not diminished by our government".
Has the Prime Minister lost control? Has he lost control of the government? I wanted to believe him. The pensioners and the parents in this country wanted to believe him. They even were willing to believe him after the 1984 election when he attempted to mess around with the pension program. But I suggest that although Canadians have now given him a second chance, a third is not likely because actions speak louder than words and this government's actions have very clearly demonstrated that the things the Prime Minister said mean nothing.

speechtext:

It being one o'clock I do now leave the chair until two o'clock this day.
