Mr. Speaker, I want to raise the concerns of the citizens of Newcastle, New Brunswick and in fact all New Brunswickers who are in a state of panic due to the series of violent deaths which have occurred there in the last few months.
These crimes have been most violent and most heinous. I understand the RCMP has assumed control of the investigation of these murders, but on the basis of the information that I have been given the RCMP has been extremely short staffed in New Brunswick due in part to its new peacekeeping role.
I am further advised that some members of the force who have an intimate knowledge of Newcastle, New Brunswick have not been utilized in the investigation due to the lack of available personnel.

I urge the minister to commit the additional staff necessary to carry out a full, complete and expeditious investigation immediately.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted with the appearance of the blue recycling boxes provided to all our offices in the House. However, I do believe that it would be much better if much of the material placed in the baskets was never produced at all.
In this time of severe budget deficits I call on every government department and agency to determine if their printed material is absolutely essential.
I believe we could all help save money, paper, the forests and energy by reducing the paper load produced by all levels of government. By doing so we can help reduce the threat to our increasingly fragile environment in a very practical way, as well as help solve our deficit problem.
*	* He

Mr. Speaker, one of the items that is always on the agenda of Commonwealth parliamentary meetings, and indeed when leaders of the Commonwealth get together, is the whole concern with respect to further decolonization.
What I would like to do today is call on the Prime Minister, while he is in that part of the world in Kuala Lumpur, to change the Canadian policy with respect to the colonization of East Timor by Indonesia, something which happened in the mid-1970s and about which Canada has been embarrassingly silent out of respect for our economic interests in Indonesia. I think it is time that this sort of thing came to an end. If we are against illegal occupation of one country by another, if we are, indeed, against genocide, as it has sometimes been called in East Timor, we ought to be against it in every case.
The Canadian record with respect to the Indonesian occupation of East Timor has been a disgrace. I call on the Prime Minister at this point to change Canadian policy, to denounce colonization and terror and genocide
wherever it occurs, and particularly at this time in East Timor.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Science and Technology)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Science and Technology)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday, I had the honour, with the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Winegard), to give out federal scholarships to university students of the Ottawa-Hull area to launch National Universities Week. This year, 3,400 two-thousand-dollar-scholarships will be granted to students across the country in science and technology related fields; 51 per cent of the recipients are women. These students will have a role to play in the future of our country since they will be tomorrow's researchers and as such, will help Canada compete in the world market. On behalf of the government and myself, I wish to congratulate the recipients and wish them the best of luck in their studies.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has told Canadians of the importance of our education system, how it will determine our competitiveness in the world, and how we must ensure first-class education for Canadians.
Despite the Prime Minister's rhetoric, the Conservative record on education is shameful. There have been deep cuts in transfer payments. There have been reductions to training and retraining programs. There have been no increases in student aid amounts. The application of the goods and services tax will include books and other learning materials. There has been embarrassingly little support for literacy.
There has been the capping of funds for the post-secondary education of natives, the elimination of the postal subsidies for scholarly journals, and the abolition of the citizenship instruction and language textbook agreement.
On Friday, October 13, I held a press conference at which I announced a challenge to the government and its ministers to discuss and debate these issues with me

October 17, 1989
across the country. Canadians want these discussions. Will these ministers participate?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce that this week, October 16 to October 20, has been proclaimed National Infection Control Week in recognition of the many health care professionals who have worked to prevent the transmission of infectious diseases in health care facilities and community based institutions.
The purpose of this week is to focus public and professional attention on both the seriousness of nosocomial and community infections and on the measures that can be taken to reduce them. I particularly applaud the efforts of the community and hospital infection control association in Canada for their efforts in sponsoring and organizing this week across Canada.
Nurses, doctors and other health care workers have long been aware of the problem and of the need for wider application of the effective infection control measures. Scientific evidence has shown that simple measures such as proper hand washing when used by everyone can reduce the spread of infection. Infection control practitioners, community health agencies and others are invited and encouraged to join CHICA Canada in promoting activities which will enhance infection control.

Mr. Speaker, it is said that a man selling doughnuts will boast about the size of the doughnuts, but the customer will consider the size of the hole.
This should be remembered when the Prime Minister tries to sell us a claim of victory for Canada's sanctions against South Africa. The hole is a big hole-the 80 per cent increase in Canada's trade with South Africa and Canada's resistance to supporting stronger sanctions.
South Africa's new velvet glove and the release of prisoners could be nicely timed to strengthen Thatcher's hand and weaken Canada's already timorous resolve at the Commonwealth Conference.
De Klerk may be simply a good card player. The Prime Minister should remember what Kenny Rogers sang: "Don't count your money while you're sitting at the table. There'll be time enough for counting when the deal is done".

Mr. Speaker, last night the Saint-Ferreol-les-Neiges Development Corporation received the Alphonse Desjardins Prize in the "Culture and Heritage" category. The Desjardins Movement thus recognized the remarkable work done by the Corporation to develop the site of the Sept-Chutes hydro-electric plant, a heritage and environmental location that nearly 50,000 people visited this summer.
Like my fellow citizens, I am very proud of this recognition because, as Corporation President Germain Tremblay said, the Government of Canada got the project going. Since 1984, our Government has spent nearly $450,000 through employment programs in Sept-Chutes.
I would like to pay tribute today to Germain Tremblay, Jean-Guy Huot, Claire Boulay and all their team for their wonderful work and I encourage them to continue for the people of Saint-Ferreol-les-Neiges and the riding of Montmorency-Orleans.

Mr. Speaker, this week is National Universities Week when we celebrate all the great things our universities do for their community, their province and their country.
The University of Prince Edward Island contributes greatly to my province and, with its new vet college, to Atlantic Canada as well. The continuing presence of the University of Prince Edward Island allows young men and women in the province to get a high quality education. A well educated workforce allows Prince Edward Island to develop as a province and to reduce its dependency on the federal government.
October 17, 1989

But by cutting funding to the provinces and to students, the federal government is condemning provinces like Prince Edward Island to a future of dependency and students to a future of debt. Education is a top priority for Islanders and I urge this government to show that it is a priority for it as well.

Mr. John A. MacDougall (Timiskaming) Mr. Speaker, in its submission to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance, the Mining Association of Canada made it known to the government that the membership supports the introduction of the GST.
Speaking for the mining community, this association sees that the new GST as a good measure. The bottom line is that mining industries which depend on the exporting of their products will benefit from the tax reforms put forward by this government.
MAC favours our tax policies because they ensure that the burden of taxes and the royalties is consistent with that in other industrialized, mineral producing countries; that taxes do not discriminate against Canadian exporters and in favour of importers; that the cost of tax compliance for industry and of administration by governments are kept reasonably low.
MAC recognizes that today's tax reform decisions made by the federal government will affect the health of the Canadian mining industry tomorrow. Its concern and our concern is to see the goods and services tax implemented and our current tax policies corrected, for the betterment of the mining sector and of individuals across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, almost five years ago the National Capital Commission announced plans and issued a contract to redevelop the Daly Building located at Sussex and Rideau Street here in Ottawa. Incredibly the start of construction on the 84-year old building is still months away.
The loss of revenue alone from tenants who should have been in the building long ago is staggering. I cannot even begin to estimate how many potential millions have been lost. I understand that problems have arisen, but for a government which claims to be the champion of fiscal restraint it is only the proving yet again that it is only the champion of rhetoric and overspending.
This fiasco must be stopped. Someone has got to put his or her foot down and take charge of the situation. I suggest that the Minister of Public Works do this. Enough time has been spent; enough money has been squandered. The NCC should put its helmets on and get into the game.
It is high time construction began so the job can be finished and we can begin making, instead of foolishly wasting, taxpayers' money.

Mr. Speaker, no one likes taxes any less than I do. I know that a large number of Canadians has already made important sacrifices to help keep the deficit under control. Together taxpayers and this government have made progress, but we still have some way to go.
The first part of sales tax reform is to remove the existing federal tax on manufactured goods. Many Canadians are unaware that since 1924 the federal sales tax has been buried in the price of every good and service produced in Canada and consumed by all Canadians. It taxes foreign made imports one-third less than it does Canadian domestically made products.
What sane country would allow such an arrangement to continue at the age of 65. It is time for the MST to retire. Then and only then will we establish the goods and services tax.
Under the GST Canadian exporters will create new jobs. Economic growth will improve living standards and contribute to bringing the deficit down.
I ask you to think about the entire package. The bad old tax out, the GST in, together with all the important fairness measures.

October 17, 1989

Mr. Speaker, last week I spoke of the ill effects of deregulation on northern Canadian communities with specific reference to skyrocketing air fares.
This week I learned that American aviation fuel is being shipped from Michigan into Canada to service Canadian aircraft, namely, Air Ontario.
If this is an isolated case-and I believe it is not-Canadian jobs are at risk for those involved in the petroleum industry. Why would Air Ontario do this? The vice-president tells me that it is to cut costs.
Pass it on to the consumers? No way. To add insult to injury and at the expense of safety, our harmonious laws permit Canadian A-l fuel to be replaced with American A fuel. The difference is simple but frightening. American fuel freezes at minus 40 degrees; Canadian fuel freezes at minus 47 degrees. What is the supposed solution? Put in an additive just like we do in our cars.
Canadians should not have to accept American fuel nor American standards. I ask the Minister to investigate this unacceptable situation immediately.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, at a press conference, the Minister of the Environment announced that the federal Government intends to spend $150 million in pollution control projects, including $100 million to clean up some 50 hazardous waste disposal sites for which the owner is unknown, cannot be found or is bankrupt.
Mr. Speaker, this announcement by the Environment Minister is very important for the people of my riding, especially in Mascouche. The Mascouche disposal site was given as an example in reports on the TVA network last night. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that my constituents are pleased with this decision, this announcement because it is a step forward; it is concrete action for environmental quality and for future generations.
I want to tell the Minister of the Environment and the House that I am fully satisfied with this announcement and I hope that the provinces will follow along at the Environment Minister's Conference this week in Charlottetown.
As for our friends opposite, who reacted to this announcement by saying it was too little too late, I will just tell them that for me and the people I represent, it is never too late and that it is much more than they did when they were able to do something.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal task force on housing, co-chaired by the Hon. Member for London East finished its cross-Canada tour of nine cities yesterday.
Nearly 70 associations submitted briefs to the task force, and it was apparent that all regions in Canada, without exception, were experiencing severe housing problems.
Whether we are talking about availability, access, the homeless or the fact that it is becoming increasingly difficult for Canadians to enjoy a right that should be theirs as a matter of course, we cannot ignore these problems.

It is unacceptable in a country such as ours that there are 1.3 million families living in unsustainable housing.
Since taking office the Conservative government has drastically cut budgets and programs. It has abandoned its responsibilities and has generally turned a blind eye to Canada's housing crisis. The new sales tax is clear evidence of this. It has made a very bad situation all the worse.

From our hearings across the country it was apparent that there is no federal leadership in this area today.

Lack of decent housing is a root cause of poverty. You may rest assured that it will be a principal focus of our report.



October 17, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I would like to put on record a short letter from Mrs. D. Simons of Orleans, Ontario, concerning abortion:
I'm ashamed to be a woman. I'm disheartened by how irresponsible, cold-hearted, and extremely selfish we have become. Led by the "women's movement", we have convinced ourselves we are not the loving, caring, nurturing beings we are by nature. We have convinced ourselves that the child in the womb is not a person worthy of respect. Were we not all a foetus in our mother's womb? Are we not the same persons we were then?
No matter how bad a woman's situation may be, she can survive, and help is there for the asking.
Mrs. Simons went on to say:
Most abortions, however, are done because the pregnancy is an embarrassment or inconvenience. Is nine months really too much to give for the life of another? Is killing your baby better than giving her to a couple who will love her as their own? Give the baby a "choice" and I'm sure she will choose life.
She concluded by saying:
I beg women to find courage to take responsibility for their actions and not take the easy way out.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Tbraer (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans about the decision of the trade panel on salmon and herring.
According to the joint statement by the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister for International Trade, and I want to quote that statement:
The Panel has accepted the legitimacy of Canada's position -the Panel has fully recognized that it is the sovereign right of Canada to decide on particular conservation policies-
So said the minister. I do not know what decision of the panel the minister has been reading. I read it carefully this morning. My copy states: "The present Canadian landing requirement cannot be said to be primarily aimed at conservation. Therefore, Canada's landing requirement is incompatible with Canada's obligations under Article 407 of the trade agreement".
Oral Questions
Does the minister have a different decision than the one that was issued by the panel, or is he relying solely on the opinion of his colleague, the Minister for International Trade who admitted to this House that he had not read the trade agreement under which the decision was made?
Having signed the deal and set up the process under which the west coast fisheries industry has now lost an important decision, why does the minister not have the courage to admit it to the fishermen of British Columbia and the country that his government blew the whole damn affair?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer the hon. Leader of the Opposition. The panel clearly upholds the sovereignty of Canada's fisheries legislation in giving to the Government of Canada and the Minister of Fisheries the authority in the final analysis to set quotas and to establish regulations from the perspective of conservation of this resource.
If the hon. member had properly read the completion of the panel finding which Canada, by the way, has not yet accepted-we have 30 days to review this question.

It is not that
good.

I would ask the hon. Leader of the Opposition to read the panel report, clause 8.02 sub. 2, where it states:
The Panel was also of the view that Canada could bring its landing requirement within Article XX (g) of the GATT, by structuring it along the lines described in paragraph 7.40.
Furthermore, if the hon. member would read from page 37 of the report-I think it is important that the House have this complete clarification-let me quote:
The panel agreed with Canada's position that a state could not be obliged to make its fisheries conservation and management regime dependent on co-operation with another state.
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the minister cried "victory". Now he says he has not finally accepted the decision.

Oh, oh!

October 17, 1989
Oral Questions

If you read the trade agreement with the United States, Articles 407 anJ 408, you will know why we lost. We gave up our right to impose an export tax which would have allowed-

Mr. Speaker, under the Free Trade Agreement, Canada, as I said just now in English, gave up its right to impose an export tax on raw fish. That is the reason for this Government's present problems. Before the FTA, Canada would have been able to take steps to protect the thousands of fishermen in our Pacific and Atlantic fisheries. Today, however, we must abide by the decision of a free trade panel, a decision that was not in our favour.
During the election campaign, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans promised our fishermen they would be protected under the FTA. What does the Minister have to say now to thousands of workers on both coasts who are going to lose their jobs in fish processing plants?
Mr. Speaker, the hon. Leader of the Opposition speaks of protection yet he is supposedly a free-trader having embraced the principle of adherence to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade-
You gave up the tax, dummy.

-and, therefore, agreeing if he were, God forbid, to be leader of this government that he would accept rulings of the GATT as we did with regard to our former unacceptable and discriminatory export restrictions.
The hon. member cannot speak out of both sides of his mouth at once.
Listen who is talking.

In fact, this free trade panel has adjudicated on a question of conservation and management and upheld the sovereignty of Canada in making those final decisions with regard to determining fisheries regulations and quotas, and that is a great gain for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the minister does not yet understand that our sole remedy
under the GATT was the export tax which his government abandoned under the trade agreement with the United States. That is why we have this problem.
On November 17, 1987, in Richmond, British Columbia, when questions were put to him by union representatives and members of the industry, the minister stated categorically, and I quote: "I give you my assurance that those jobs are safe". Those were his words as he referred to the workers in the fish processing industry on the west coast.
Yesterday, his response to the same question from a journalist about the same jobs was this, and I quote him again: "It is really not appropriate that you ask such an over-simplified question and expect a categorical answer".
Well, Mr. Speaker, two years ago he guaranteed that those jobs would be saved, now he says, "don't ask me, it is too complicated".
Why did the Minister break his word or is this question too over simplified for him to answer?
Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Mr. Speaker, the question is certainly over simplified coming from where it arises.
Oh, oh!
But I can certainly answer the question. In the free trade era we are seeing untold increases in the numbers of jobs in Canada and in British Columbia.
Hear, hear!
Not in fisheries.

Subsection 2 states: "Until an amendment to the Constitution of Canada is made in relation to the Senate pursuant to Section 41, of the Constitution Act, 1982, the person summoned to fill a vacancy in the Senate shall be chosen from among the persons whose names have been submitted under Subsection 1, by the government of the

One of the things that is very noticeable in Canada is that we have changing demographics and our birth rate is dropping. At the same time, the cost of raising children has increased dramatically. This program has tied families together because every family, regardless of economic circumstances, has had one common universal program which they know they will all receive.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from Surrey. It is important when we talk about the impact of the clawback in family allowance on the family that we think about it in terms of the whole context of the attack on the family that is being carried out by this government.
We have an attack on the family under the unemployment insurance program. We have an attack on the family in terms of an attack on pensions of seniors who are part of the expanded family. We have an attack on the family with the clawback on the family allowance.
We are facing today an amendment to this legislation that will mean that any family with an income of $50,000 will see a portion of its family allowance clawed back.
Again, expanding and projecting what this clawback will mean in 20 years, one need only take a look at the impact on pensions and transfer it to family allowances. This means that in many cases the family allowance currently going into a home is the only independent income that a mother has in terms of spending for her

children or spending for the home, and it is going to be taxed based on her husband's income. It is a total denial of the universality in which this family allowance program was introduced. Mr. Speaker, I rise today to address this House on Bill C-28, an act to amend the Income Tax Act, the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act, the Old Age Security Act, the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act, the War Veterans Allowance Act and a related Act.
This piece of legislation is a myriad of amendments to the Income Tkx Act, some 59 amendments aimed at implementing most of the provisions detailed in the government's April, 1989 Budget, a budget that pum-meled Canadian families, insulted the voters of this country and penalized the poor even further.
This legislation continues, or more appropriately, cements the government's plan to end the universality of social programs. We know that the government's social program cuts will make up nearly 30 per cent, or $610 million of the $2.8 billion in spending cuts. The Minister of Finance announced these cuts for the 1990-91 fiscal year. This was in addition to the previously proposed changes to the unemployment insurance program which will eliminate the government's contribution of $1.9 billion in the year 1990-91.
We are seeing the end of universality, a long standing principle of the Canadian system of social benefits. I say that because universality is by definition of or belonging to or done by all persons or things in the world or in the class concerned and is applicable to all cases. In other words, regardless of income some benefits have to be delivered to everyone. What the government is proposing in this legislation is to take away all of the benefits
Government Orders
over a specific income level, not only for old age security pensions, but for family allowances as well.
Canadians have long been told to consider old age pensions when planning for their retirement. Now they find that the pensions will not be there as expected, and that at this time they have very little chance of changing their financial situation. What happened to the Prime Minister's position of 1984 when he promised that universality was a sacred trust? That sacred trust has been tossed aside by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and this government as a whole.
In 1984 the then Minister of National Health and Welfare stated in the House: "All savings generated from any changes will be redistributed to social programs and will not be applied to deficit reduction". He went on to say: "Benefits from old age pensions will be taxed no differently from any other form of income".
It is not hard to understand why Canadians are angry at this government. I guess the sacred trust has been replaced with the other two words we have had drilled into us lately, those of "deficit reduction". If the senior citizens of this country, individuals who have given many years of hard work and trust, cannot be spared by this government then I guess it is obvious that aside from major corporations no one will be spared.
Bill C-28 brings more tax increases, reduced federal transfers to the provinces for health and post-secondary education and imposes clawbacks on family allowances and old age security benefits, specifically Part 1.2 of Clause 48 of the legislation which implements these clawbacks. The clawback of the family allowances will take $1,686 billion out of the budgets of Canadian families over the next five years. Due to partial indexing, close to one million Canadian families who currently receive family allowances or old age pensions will begin to lose these benefits within ten years.
These clawbacks are anti-family and anti-senior. No matter what the total income for a senior citizen is, the principle of fairness suggests that it should not matter how a person attains this income. It should not matter whether it came from the government or from financial investments. The government's clawback would single out certain groups of people who receive family allowance or old age pension cheques for a special tax. Seniors

October 17, 1989
Government Orders
who receive their income from a pension will pay more tax than seniors who receive their income from investments. This is simply unjust.
Under the aforementioned tax changes family allowances and old age pensions will be taxed from individuals with net incomes over $50,000, not from families. The clawback system is set up in such a way as to allow a family in which each parent or partner works and earns $49,000 to retain all of its benefits because neither individual alone earns over $50,000. In stark contrast, a family in which one parent or partner works and earns $75,000 will lose all of its family allowance or old age pension benefits to the government's clawback system.
In the government's own consultation paper entitled "Child and Elderly Benefits" January, 1985, the idea of clawback on old age benefits was rejected. It stated that it would seriously disrupt the retirement income system.
The fine print of this legislation states that the $50,000 threshold between those who must pay the surtax and those who do not will be indexed each year according to increases in the Consumer Price Index, but at less than 3 per cent. If incomes continue to increase in keeping with the rate of inflation, but the threshold rises less than 3 per cent, then families and seniors will quickly fall to the other side of the ledger and have to pay the surtax.
The Minister of Finance has stated that the government will occasionally restore the threshold since it is only partially indexed. Does he really mean this? He does not seem to realize what universality means, so one can only assume what he thinks "occasionally" means. Perhaps to the minister, 31 tax increases in five years is occasional. If so, it seems he will adjust the threshold, but don't be surprised if no adjustments are forthcoming.
Parents and pensioners make a special, invaluable contribution to our society, in the past, present and future. These clawbacks imply that such contributions are unimportant and that some are worth even less than others. The families and seniors of this country deserve better treatment and more respect than this. We in the Liberal party do not believe in treating valuable members of our society the way that this government is treating them.
At a recent convention of the National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation, an umbrella organization for seniors' groups in Canada, members voted unanimously to bring a court challenge against the government clawback. They are furious not only because their incomes will be taxed at a higher rate, but because the minister refuses to fully index the $50,000 threshold, a situation which must give him a sense of deja vu.
A clawback on old age security pensions will force 54,000 seniors to pay back all of their pensions. Furthermore, 74,000 seniors have to pay back at least some portion of their pensions. How is this government going to explain to seniors why it has taken contributions that were made in good faith? Seniors paid into the program and they have a right to reap the benefits.
Canadians are going to fight this government. We in the Liberal party will fight this government to stop the continued erosion of the very fabric of this nation. We have seen a flood of regressive policies from this government, VIA Rail cuts, unemployment insurance cuts, and base closures that have devastated regions such as my province of Prince Edward Island. They assure us that it is all for our own good. Now we face clawbacks, and the government could never generate enough rhetoric to mask its long hand reaching further and further into the very heart of Canada until it is tom right out.
Canadians cannot trust this government. They are being cheated out of what belongs to them. They are being betrayed after years of contributing to the society in good faith. This legislation is an insult to every man, woman and child, every family and eveiy senior in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to rise and speak on Bill C-28, an act to amend the Income Thx Act, the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act, the Old Age Security Act, the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act, the War Veterans Allowance Act and a related Act. On the various components of this bill I would like to focus my comments in opposition specifically to that which relates to the Old Age Security Act. I therefore rise and speak out against this bill because it proposes amendments which will result in a move away from our tradition of universality in social programs. This is the most significant change in social policy in a generation in Canada.
Part 1.2 of Clause 48 on page 46, Section 180.2 of the bill as printed is entitled "Tax on Family Allowances and Old Age Security Benefits". This particular part implements the clawback of family allowances and Old Age Security pensions. Henceforth individuals earning more than $70,000 will no longer receive old age pensions and family allowances. Those earning $70,000 will receive partial old age pensions and family allowances. The tax-back rate will be 15 per cent. The $50,000 threshold will be partially deindexed. In real terms the threshold will be reduced through time. This measure will be phased in over three years. When fully phased in, the tax

October 17, 1989
Government Orders
increase will be much higher than the $320 million reported by the government.
This clawback is not only unfair and dangerous to universality, but it is a blatant example of the pernicious way this government runs the country. The government said one thing during an election campaign, made all sorts of promises to win votes, and then as soon as it was re-elected it ignores the concerns and neglects the needs of Canadians. It abandons, or, worse, it dismantles social programs which are put in place to promote the social and economic interests of all Canadians, families and seniors included.
This is intolerable. This government is no longer just cutting the fat from our social programs. It is cutting the sinew, the muscle, and even the bone of our social character, of our social well-being. This government is trying to destroy the very foundation of our society by attacking the universality of social programs and by unfairly targeting groups, such as senior citizens who are the most vulnerable to attack, who made it possible for us to be where we are today.
What is particularly frightening is that this government refuses to index the $50,000 threshold for the first 3 per cent of each year's inflation. If we look ahead at maintaining current buying power while evaluating seniors' income in constant dollars, and if we project current inflation rates forward, in eight years the threshold will be the equivalent of only $35,000 or $40,000. By the year 2000, the clawback will start at $35,765; in 15 years from now, the threshold will be down to $30,000; and five years later, when the first of the baby boomers start retiring, it will stand at only $28,000 a year and will affect 2 million Canadians. Eventually the number of Canadians returning their entire benefits to the taxman will be so large that the idea of making payments to everyone will be abandoned. That then will be the demise of universality.
The clawback tax is also frightening because it is unfair. The impact will not only be confined to high-income Canadians, it will discriminate against one-income families and against senior citizens 65 years of age and older. A family with one net income of $55,240 will have to pay back all of its family allowances as a result of this
new amendment. But a two-income family, in which one spouse earns $45,000 and the other some $40,000 will not have to pay back anything. By any arithmetic standard the proposed clawback cannot even approximate fan-taxation.
The seniors' clawback amounts to age discrimination, since a pensioner earning $60,000 a year will be treated differently by the income tax system than a 64-year-old. Further, the clawback will single out those people who receive family allowance and old age pension for a special tax; such that seniors who receive their income from a pension only will pay more tax than seniors who receive their income from investments.
The clawback is unfair, in fact, unethical for another reason. The elderly have already paid for their old age pensions through a lifetime of paying income taxes. The clawback changes the rules of the game without the consent of those who had paid in the past.
In the 1950s the government insisted Old Age Security would be a contributory plan that paid for itself with each year's benefits funded by matching contributions. A special tax was created for the purpose, and each time the pension was raised the tax was raised. Seniors of today paid for that tax.
That tax was not ended until the 1972 tax reform. Hence seniors, because they had made their contributions, have a legal, moral, and ethical right to collect this pension. For years people have been told to consider old age pensions when planning their retirement income. Now they may find out that it may not always be there at a time when they have little chance of changing their financial situation.
The elderly are also in a poor position to fight back against a government that is whittling away at then-pensions. They cannot afford to hire an expert who can help them to file their forms and show them how to reduce their taxes. They are being cheated by this government's clawback scheme out of the pension they have paid for in the past. This is exactly what the Prime Minister promised not to do during the last election campaign. Indeed, in the presence of his mother, the Prime Minister promised that any government he would lead would improve pensions rather than degrade them.
October 17, 1989

The government swore during its election campaign that social benefits would not be jeopardized and that old age pensions were a sacred trust. Suddenly, after the election, statements about sacred trusts are being replaced by statements about the need to decrease the deficit. The government knew, or ought to have known, the state of the financial books at that time. Yet the government chose not to tell the Canadian people then. Now the government is stating that all Canadians, including seniors, have a responsibility to pay out of their own pockets to make up for this government's fiscal ineptitude. This, I submit, is a blatant breach of faith. The government has gone about breaking its word in a very insidious manner. This government claims that it is continuing the principle of universality but in reality it is cancelling it. It does not even have the courage to be honest with the Canadian people.

Part 1.2 under clause 48 implements the clawback of family allowance, the clawback of old age security pensions. It will take from Canadian families $1.68 billion of their budgets in the next five years, or the government will clawback $500 million a year from our seniors and from our families.

The deindexing of the $50,000 threshold means that within 10 years close to one million Canadian families will start losing their family allowances and old age pensions. The clawback proposal would put a special tax on families with children and on seniors.
I mean by "a special tax" an inequitable tax and unfair tax because it does not apply to anyone else. You have to be a senior or have entitlements to family allowance to have this tax applied to you. It does not take very much logic to understand that this clawback is anti-family and anti-senior.
How can Canadians trust someone who in front of the cameras in the last election made a solemn promise to his mother-remember that one-never to touch universality. A few months later he turns his back on his own mother and abolishes universality. We have developed in this country over the years a great system of social programs. All Canadians have universal access on a non-profit basis. Whether you can afford it or not you will get fair, equitable and good treatment in our hospitals and in the health care system.
You will get a pension; it does not matter if you are from the east or the west, tall or short, fat or whatever, you get the same pension whether you are rich or poor. That is what is called universality. That is why the National Council of Welfare said in its report published in September:

them all back from some recipients is not universal.
It appears to me that it is a very simple argument. Why is the government proposing today to tax seniors and family allowance recipients in a different manner than it taxes other people? I tell you that is wrong.

Mr. Speaker, normally when there is significant change in social policy governments come forward with a White Paper or a royal commission and say up front that they have decided to change the social contract within a country.
One of the things that surprises me is that this government is probably making one of the most significant changes in our social policy, certainly since the end of the Second World War, and it is doing so while at the same time trying to deny that it is taking place. But then again, I am beginning to understand that what the government says and what the government does are two entirely different things. It says it is going to improve the Unemployment Insurance Act when in fact it is diminishing the benefits available to a large number of people and starting the dismantling of the unemployment insurance system.
It is going to improve VIA Rail by doing away with half of it. Now it is introducing a fundamental change in the Canadian social security system without ever even acknowledging that this is what is taking place.
This bill deals with two fundamentalist aspects. One is the whole question of universality of social programs and the other is the credibility of this government, particularly the credibility of the Prime Minister. On both counts the government seems to be determined not to acknowledge that this is what is taking place.
I cannot help but think that much of what we are seeing in this legislation is outflowing from the free trade deal. During the debate on the free trade deal and the discussion during the 1988 election campaign, the government insisted over and over again that the free trade deal would not affect our social programs; that it would not affect our programs like unemployment insurance, health care, pensions and family allowances; that these were programs that would have no impact from the free
trade deal. Yet, as soon as the free trade deal was ratified we found out that all these programs were under attack.
There is a harmonization taking place between the social programs in the United States and the social programs in Canada. This means that there is a fundamental change taking place in Canada. The United States has a free market concept even in the area of social programs, that is, the wealthy and the powerful can take care of themselves and then they set up a charity for those who fall between the cracks, those who are unprotected-the weak, the poor and the disadvantaged-and provide them with a few minimal crumbs.
Canada has taken a different approach. We have said there are some social benefits in this country that go to all citizens. We have outlined these. Pensions for the elderly is one area that I will come back to on a number of occasions. The concept is a universal program to which every elderly person based on their citizenship, not on their race, colour, creed, wealth, income, or anything else, is entitled. That is universality.
We have established family allowance, again quite unique from the United States. The United States has no universal family allowance program. We say that every child as a right of Canadian citizenship is entitled to receive family allowance. It is not dependent upon them being from Vancouver, Halifax or Yukon. It is not dependent upon their parents being educated or uneducated. It is not dependent upon their parents being multi-millionaires or are eking out a living. We have said that we have a concept of universality and this bill attacks those two programs.
Let us also take a look at our other universal programs in Canada. As sure as this government succeeds in doing away with universality of those two social programs, it will do away with the universality of other programs.
Let us take a look at them. First, our health care system. The concept is diametrically different from what it is in the United States. There is no universal health care, particularly hospital care, available to those in the United States.
In Canada there is. One of the fundamental rights of being a Canadian citizen is that one is entitled to health care as a universal program.
October 17, 1989

Education is a fundamental right. It is a universal program in Canada. We have universal unemployment insurance in Canada. The United States does not have any universal unemployment insurance program. What we see now is the government attacking these programs.
Before I go into detail about the pension and family allowance, I want to explain how it is starting to attack the universality of the other programs. Let me take as an example the health care system. The health care system in this country is deteriorating badly. In my own riding of Surrey North we have a crisis. The Surrey hospital is dramatically underfunded. The publicly elected board was suspended some time ago. The public has been kept from involvement in that hospital in order to cover up the difficulties that are emerging in the deterioration of health care. Clearly, part of that is the responsibility of the Vander Zalm government, but the federal Conservative government is also responsible. It has been systematically reducing the transfer payments for health care to the provinces. Last year it reduced it by 2 per cent. This year it has a companion bill to this piece of legislation that will reduce it by another 1 per cent. This is in spite of inflation in the area of health care.
There is a deterioration in the funding level for health care from this government and from the provincial government. In an area like Surrey North, which is one of the fastest growing areas in Canada, there simply is not the funds to maintain the services, let alone the expansion that is necessary in order to meet the growing population.
We have some very ludicrous situations happening in Surrey North. We built a hospital complex, but the two levels of government do not provide the funding for the staffing of it. We now have a situation where the people in Surrey North are disentitled to the universality of health care. They do not get the same health care as one gets in Vancouver or in Montreal or in Toronto. This is a method of eroding universal programs.
The same thing can be said in terms of the decision to opt for two-tiered health care systems. Within the province of British Columbia the government has been sending up trial balloons by proposing that perhaps there should be certain kinds of medical services available to those who can afford it. We now have private clinics

springing up. Instead of having to wait for a public bed hospital one can go in and pay if one can pay the full cost.
One system for the rich and another for the poor.

That is right. We are not getting universality but one system for the rich and another for the poor.
The same thing is happening in education, which is another universal program. We have a whole series of private educational facilities, even at the elementary level, springing up. As the funding for the public school system is kept down, the calibre and quality of the system deteriorates. Those who have money opt for a private system, particularly when it is funded 75 per cent or 80 per cent by public dollars and all they have to do is throw in the extra 20 per cent.
What we have in this bill is the beginning of the erosion of universality of our social programs. I think it is appropriate that we remind ourselves of the old story of the Arabs and the camel in the tent. The camel sticks his nose in the tent and says all he wants is for his nose to get warm. Of course, when you allow his nose in, then he puts his neck, his front quarters and his hind quarters in and then he forces you out of the tent. The Conservatives have learned that if they tried up front by a major policy decision to say that they were doing away with the concept of universality of social programs in Canada, there would be an uprising in this country, so they are going to do it incrementally, incrementally, incrementally-
Maybe the only Conservative who is honest and upright about this change is the hon. member for Mississauga South, otherwise known as the chairman of the finance committee of the House. He says clearly that it is eliminating universality and yes, it is unfair and yes, it is sneaky. But he is the only one that is willing to admit that yes, it is unfair and yes, it is sneaky. What is behind this bill is a sneaky attack on the major element of social programs in this country, that of universality.
One of the things that we should also continue to remember is that this is an attack on the credibility of the government and particularly the credibility of the Prime Minister. When you look at the statements of the Prime Minister, it is almost incomprehensible that we could be standing here in this House debating this type of a bill. In March, 1984 he said our position is simple and straight-

Government Orders
forward, we are in favour of universality in social programs and it shall not be touched. How do you get from that statement to this legislation if it is not a sneaky move?
Again, when he was talking to the seniors in October, 1988, during the election, he said: "Let me say a special word to the senior citizens. In the future Canada, we'll be doing more, not less, for all of you". Get the words, "we'll be doing more, not less, for all of you". He did not qualify that by saying for all of you earning under $50,000 or for all of you earning under $40,000 in 10 years. He said,"for all of you. As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada, social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved, not diminished by our government which is committed to social justice and fairness for Canadians". How do you get from that statement to today? Sneaky.
What we have here is not only an attack on seniors and families, but an attack on all of our social programs. Maybe the most unfortunate thing for Canada in the long run is that we have had an attack on the credibility of government. People are becoming not only sceptical, they are totally disillusioned. How can you accept a Prime Minister standing up and saying clearly, unequivocally, that we are going to increase programs for the elderly, for all people, and then bringing in a piece of legislation like this?
I want to touch briefly on the substance of the bill because I think the substance of the clawback system has been discussed in the House. I am sure others will deal with some of the technical parts of the bill. Basically we are saying that, because we are going to be only partially indexing the clawback system over the next few years, more and more seniors will lose all of their old age pensions. Who is to say next year that the government will not decide it is $40,000 maximum and the following year $30,000? Once the camel has its nose in the door of the tent, who is going to stop it? I say we stop it now.
If any people accept the statements of the Prime Minister as guarantees, then they are really living in fantasyland. Next year, why is it not going to be $40,000 or $30,000 as the threshold? Do you believe the Prime Minister because he says $50,000 is the limit? No. What
we have is the beginning of the erosion of our universal system. They cannot even get the technical parts of it right. A family is not even considered a family unit. A one wage earner family is treated differently than a two wage earner family. At least if you are doing away with universality, get the technical parts of it right.
I want to just turn, in my last three or four minutes, to some of the alternatives. This change is being made in the name of deficit reduction. Everything that the Conservatives are doing, they say that it is because we need deficit reduction. There are many better ways to reduce the deficit, and I will just mention a couple of them.
All you have to do is increase the personal income tax rate for the highest income tax bracket by 1 per cent and you would gain the same amount of money that you would get in the clawback of family allowance and old age pensions. If you were a little bit brave and decided that you were going to increase the tax rate from 29 per cent to 32 per cent, you could in fact dramatically reduce the deficit by $2.5 million.
What we now have is, I think, a very quick sleight of hand taking place by the Conservatives. They are again protecting their friends in the wealthy group. If they raised the tax for all Canadians in wealthy groups, they would have to pay considerably more money than what they will lose in terms of the clawback on family allowance.
I just want to finish with one quick statement. Every organization, the seniors, people representing the Canadian Council of Social Development, have all been very, very clear that this is the end of universality. If the government really believes that it is best for Canada to do away with universal social programs, then at least conservatives should have the honesty and integrity to stand up in this House and say, "We believe that universal programs should be done away with and that is why we are bringing in this legislation."

Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment my colleague from Surrey North on his comments. At the beginning of his remarks he made reference to the trade deal with the United States. How does he see the impact of the trade deal on the attack on our social programs in Canada today?
October 17, 1989

Mr. Speaker, during the election and the trade debate in the fall of 1988, the government kept insisting that there was nothing in the free trade deal that was going to put pressure on the harmonization of social programs. Immediately the deal is consummated, we find that all of the social programs are being attacked, and they are being attacked in a manner that is going to bring them into harmony with the programs in the United States. They are reducing unemployment insurance. They are doing away with the universal old age pensions. They are scrapping universal family allowances. They are starting to erode our health care system so that we are going to end up with a patchwork health care system like the United States has.
They keep saying that, "we are just doing this because of the deficit", when the reality is that they knew that as soon as they consummated that deal, unless they started to harmonize our social programs, the United States had already served notice on them that it would bring forward actions to have our social programs deemed to be an unfair trade advantage, a subsidy under the free trade deal.
The government is not even willing to take the chance of going through that process and possibly losing at the end. It is taking the attitude that in case we lose, we might as well capitulate. We have seen that in fish. We did not even fight for it, we just gave up our whole processing industry in British Columbia. It is happening in steel.
One of the things they keep saying is that we are not doing it because of the free trade deal, we are doing it because of the deficit. A family that is earning over $100,000 is going to lose $270 per child by this clawback system. Let them keep their family allowance, tax it at a normal rate, but let us increase that marginal tax rate for the wealthy of 29 per cent to 32 per cent and that family would pay $2,250. This government has bought its rich friends another $2,000 in an unfair tax advantage.

Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat shocked and dismayed that the government would move so quickly to stifle debate on the bill before us today. It is a bill that is going to inflict unknown hardship on the elderly of this country and on those who worked to build this country to make it the great nation that it is today. To move so quickly to shut off debate on this contentious piece of legislation is not in the best interests of the people of Canada, and is taking away from the retirement of our seniors. It will inflict hardships on them that are not acceptable in today's society.
While I welcome the chance to add my voice to the torrent of those who are opposed to the bill, it is with regret that I rise to speak on this matter. Many people of this country believed the Prime Minister's claim that universality is a sacred trust. Further, I loathe seeing how his actions reflect on the respect that the people have for this House, for all members of Parliament and for the truth, as I am sure some of the members opposite are beginning to understand. The actions of the government in introducing this legislation reflect very poorly on all members, on Parliament itself, and on the very idea that this is an institution of truth and respect. Never before has the Prime Minister so blatantly stated one thing during a general election less than a year ago and done quite the opposite almost immediately thereafter.
In fact, on October 16, 1988, when in Summerside, he told the citizens of Summerside, P.E.I.:
As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved and not diminished by our government.
When in Summerside, did the Prime Minister tell the truth? Did he go on to attempt to explain that he would introduce a clawback, a mechanism that would slowly eat away at the very social benefits he said he would improve? Of course not, because he knew the people of Summerside and the people of Canada would recognize the truth behind his words, that he fully intended to dismantle universality.
Did the Prime Minister of Canada tell the people of Summerside that if re-elected, the next budget he would bring in would shut down their town, that he would move the armed forces base, that he would close down half of the passenger rail service in this country, that he would attempt to make unemployment insurance unworkable? Did he say that he would remove the underpinnings of the orderly marketing systems, that he would trade away
October 17, 1989

the very livelihoods of farm people behind closed doors, that he would close up a total of 14 military bases? No.
He spoke of the free trade agreement. He said that it would ensure our social programs. The truth was, he was assuring corporate America with the free trade agreement, that we would remove those social programs because our neighbours to the south had nothing to compare with them.
Did he speak of the huge national debt that his government had inflated in the last five years? Did he say the deficit had increased in the last two years from $28 billion in 1987 to $29 billion in 1988-89 and to $30.5 billion in 1989-90? Did he say that the free trade agreement would cost the government $10 billion in lost excise revenue in a year and that that money would have to come from somewhere? It is obvious that some of it will be coming from the scrapping of the universality of our social programs, from a new tax on nearly all goods and services.
Did he mention that his government in five years is responsible for 50 per cent of the national debt since Confederation? No. He and his Minister of Finance hid the truth like a candle under a basket until November 22. They knew the economic record they had created and they knew how dismal that record really was. They knew they would push interest rates up, that they would overvalue our dollar. Even now the Minister of Finance would rather go to court than lift the basket, and release those studies that a newspaper applied for under the Access to Information Act, acting in direct contravention of that act.
The government neglected to point out that as every year passes, pensions become less and less secure and social programs will be less and less universal. The threshold today is $50,000, as outlined in the legislation. By the year 2000, if the clawback is left as it is, it will have fallen to the equivalent of $35,000. It will affect almost 30 per cent of all families that receive family allowance; that is, if the government does not accelerate the rate of the clawback.
The Prime Minister said this would not happen. But look at recent history in the country. The finance
Government Orders
minister said when the individual surtax was introduced that it was temporary. Now this bill will make it permanent and raise it from 3 per cent to 5 per cent. The government said the clawback will not be increased, the goods and services tax will not rise from 9 per cent to 13.5 per cent like the present sales tax has under its stewardship. Yet taxes have increased 31 times under this government since September, 1984.
I remember on June 17, 1987, that the Minister of Finance told the country that when the new sales tax is introduced, the personal and corporate surtaxes will be removed. The Minister of Finance has introduced his sales tax so where is the bill to back up his 1987 statement? Where is the clause that removes, as promised, the temporary surtax? What does history show for the future, more of what we have seen since 1984? Does it show the clawback will not be accelerated, the general sales tax will not be accelerated, the once temporary surtax will not be accelerated? I think it shows quite the opposite, despite any assurance the government may offer at this point to the people of Canada.
The clawback is nothing more than a licensed theft. If a private corporation attempted to treat their old age pensions like this legislation is going to treat the old age security, they would be breaking the law. Canadians who paid tax in the early 1950s to 1971 paid a special surtax for their pensions. In fact, the 1979 tax guide stated: "All taxpayers whose taxable income is over $500 are subject to the old age security tax". To take this money back now on their old age security is the equivalent to theft, and the government wants to steal back some of that money. Just a little now, it says, as if that makes it okay.
What is being taken away is the very principle of universality, the principle that our tax system should be fair, a principle that is outlined in this bill and a principle that is depended on by scores of elderly here in Canada.
The chairman of the finance committee knows it. It is what he told his constituents. In a recent letter to one of his constituents he said:
We have decided to eliminate universality, and we do that in a sense that by the clawback in both family allowance and old age pensions. As you know, it has been a Conservative philosophy for some time that distributions from state ought to go essentially to those in need. While the clawback may be unfair and sneaky it is there.

The clawback, like this government, is both unfair and sneaky, and the actions of the government are uncovering the candle of truth it tried to hide with its words. The government's actions admit what it did not say prior to November 21, 1988. It still will not admit that the government decided a long time ago to eliminate universality, to shut down VIA Rail, to undermine orderly marketing, to privatize unemployment insurance and to cutback universal medicare, and in so doing, change the Canada we have known for the last 122 years.
In that last 122 years since Confederation, Canada has developed as a nation of compassion, a caring nation, a nation that has cared for the elderly and less fortunate, a nation with a safety net that was available to society, a safety net that provided for health care so the elderly could live their retirement free of worry and want, a life of dignity. This bill will strip that dignity away from the elderly and the less fortunate of Canada, today and in the future. This bill is wrong, the clawback is wrong, the government is wrong.

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Lambton- Middlesex. I think it is very important that we remember that what is happening here flies, as he said, in direct contradiction to the commitments this government made when it was out on the hustings looking for votes. There are a few aspects of the hon. member's remarks that I would like him to expand on a bit.
First, this government tries to persuade Canadians that one of its top priorities is to reinforce family life. I was wondering whether the member might comment on the effect of the particular approach they have taken to the clawback on the family allowances. A family with two incomes gets taxed in a much different way than a family with just one income, even if that income is at the same level. I would ask the member to comment on that.
Second, I would like to ask the member to comment on the fact that the government apparently sees this as a deficit reduction measure, a way to save money and deal with the fiscal problems of this country. I wonder if the member might comment on the justice that is involved in clawing back pensions and the family allowances as opposed to using other sources of revenue which the
government might look to in order to solve its fiscal problems.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. colleague for the question. Perhaps I should deal with the family allowance portion of his question first. I am sure that he has a similar situation in his riding as I do in mine. My riding is a predominantly rural riding.
Because of government policies over the last few years, the farm income has dropped dramatically to the point where many farm families have husbands and wives both who have to seek off-farm employment in order to keep the farm operational and in order to subsidize the farm income. Having a clawback apply to their family allowances hits them extremely hard, because the money that they anticipated putting away for their children's education, money that they anticipated would be available for them to buy clothes, to buy food and the finer things in life, will no longer be available to them. In effect, what is happening here is they are robbing Peter to pay Paul. I think this is wrong. The people who are having, for example, to work off their farms, moonlighting if you want to call it that, in order to make ends meet and have large incomes that are being used as subsidies, should not be subjected to this. It is very unfair that this should have to take place in society as we know it today.
In terms of the deficit reduction, I do not think it is at all fair that the government should try to fight the deficit on the backs of the elderly and the less advantaged of this countiy. As I mentioned a few moments earlier, Canada is looked upon as a caring nation, a nation that looks after the disadvantaged and the people who do not have the same opportunities in one region as they do in another. I think it is blatantly unfair of the government to make such a move as this to try to fight the deficit. The deficit has been increasing and will continue to increase as long as the balance of trade continues to slip, not in favour of Canada, but in favour of our trading partners. Therefore, it is blatantly unfair that the older and the less advantaged in this country should be burdened with having to fight a deficit such as this government is running today.

Mr. Speaker, with great respect, I think that there is a tradition in this House that a minister be present in the chamber during discussion of government bills. That is the point I am trying to make. It seems to me, Sir, that that is an obligation.
We had a few minutes ago the spectacle of the Minister of National Health and Welfare waltzing into this House, standing up and indicating that he was going to move closure, then waltzing out again. No other Parliament in Canadian history has been so burdened with closure the way this Parliament has been under this Conservative administration, the fumbling and bumbling of which has resulted in this dreadful bill that we are debating today.
I can understand the Conservatives anxiety to rush the bill through because they do not want the people of Canada to hear how bad this bill is. They feel that if they can move closure on the bill and ramrod it through this Parliament, then there will not be speeches on the bill through which they as ministers will have to sit. The Conservatives know what we are saying is true. They do not want the Canadian people to listen to speeches that indicate the faults of this bill because Canadians might believe it and, the next time they get a chance, will vote this group out of office. Well they should, Mr. Speaker. There is ample reason for that on the basis of what we have heard today alone.

The Minister of Fisheries is mumbling things from his seat. I invite him to participate in this debate and make his voice heard. Perhaps tomorrow night at one o'clock in the morning he can tell us about it.
Speak on the bill.

I intend to turn to the bill.
I want to make certain points, Mr. Speaker, with respect to the clawback provisions of this bill because that, in my respectful submission, is the most important and evil part of the legislation. It affects Canada's seniors and I am going to deal with that aspect of it. I am not going to deal with the clawback of family allowances although, as I will say at the end, most of the comments I make on the one could be applied mutatis mutandis to the other. I will stick to the clawback of the pensions, and I want to say certain things about that which I think are important.
First, the question of a clawback, in my view, is manifestly unfair. Speaker after speaker on this side, of the few we have had on this debate, certainly, and those on the budget when it was debated, have indicated the unfairness of this provision. Our leader, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, in his initial address on this bill indicated his objection to this particular clawback arrangement.
I reiterate that one of the problems with the clawback is manifested by this example. I will indicate a suggestion to Your Honour and see if Your Honour does not agree with me that this bill is unfair in its application and in its treatment of the senior citizens of this country.
Ihke the position of a senior citizen residing in his own home, fully paid for-the Conservative dream I am sure. It is certainly the dream that we on this side of the House have espoused for Canadians-mortgage free, it is a valuable piece of real estate that is increasing in value every year. His income, including his old age pension, in our example is $50,000. Imagine if after a year or two this senior citizen becomes incapable of continuing to live alone in this home. The house is then put on the market and sold for, say, $300,000. If the person is living in Toronto, that would be easy. It would not be a very great home for $300,000 in the Toronto real estate market the way things have gone under this government.
The senior citizen sells the home, takes the $300,000 and invests the money at, say, 10 per cent. Then his income goes from $50,000 to $80,000. Clawback! That senior citizen loses the pension and moves into rental accommodation. Is that fair? Why should the senior

October 17, 1989
Government Orders
citizen be penalized for moving into rental accommodation because the person is unable to continue to reside in his own home? Yet that is the effect of this legislation which the government has introduced.
Check the facts.

I have checked the facts with the hon. member for Etobicoke North, my colleague. He knows the facts and he is well aware of what is in this bill. If the Minister of Fisheries disagrees with my assessment he should make a speech because I am right, and he knows I am right on this point.
The clawback will set in and the senior will be deprived of the income from that pension. Mr. Speaker, you are a man of sense. You must agree that this particular provision is unfair, unreasonable and ought to be stricken from the bill.
In addition, I invite you to consider the costs of this particular system. The government says that universality is a sacred trust, pensions are a sacred trust so we do not want to breach our obligation to the electorate. They tried and there was such an outcry that the Prime Minister himself backed off and ordered the Minister of Finance to recant his heresy and withdraw the changes to the old age security pension that were introduced in the Parliament before this one.
Now instead of trying to do it by the front door, the Conservatives are doing it by the back door. Instead of taking away the pension, they say that they will give you the pension but they will tax it all back. That is what they are doing. That is what this is all about.
I want to take a look at the costs of this little proposal of theirs. I have taken a quick glance, with assistance, at the Estimates. I did a quick calculation. I went into the Estimates and I looked at the cost of administering the Department of National Revenue. I looked at the cost of the taxation branch which amounted to the pretty sizeable figure of $946 million. That is what it costs to administer the tax system in this country. That is for all the tax police. I took 80 per cent of that, because 80 per cent of the combined personal and corporate taxation is, in fact, personal taxes in this country. Eighty per cent of
the $946 million yielded a total cost of $757 million to administer the income tax portion of our tax system.
That does not include-I want to stress this-the administrative superstructure of the Department of National Revenue; the minister and his car allowance, the deputy ministers and their allowances, the various administrative personnel at the top of the department who do not specifically assign any portion of their costs to this taxation branch. If you do that simple arithmetical calculation on budget figures, not on actuals, I think you will find the cost of raising a tax dollar in Canada is about 7.5 cents. For every dollar the government raises it pays out 7.5 cents to collect it.
Then I did a similar analysis for the cost of paying out the old age pension. The government administers pensions worth almost $12 billion per year according to the 1989-90 Estimates. The costs of administration of those pensions, again according to its Estimates and again without any of the superstructure of the Department of National Health and Welfare, amounted to about $56.35 million. So, the cost of paying out the money to the Government of Canada in the form of old age security pension cheques amounts to 2.1 cents for every dollar paid out.
Under this new scheme, the money is not taxed in once, it is taxed in twice, because the government is going to tax the money first, pay it out and then tax it all back. In fact, you have to double the cost of collection from 7.5 cents to 15 cents and add the 2 cents on for the payment out. You get about 17 cents for every old age security tax dollar that is dealt with in this double-barrelled system the government is proposing.
I know the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans will be working these figures out in his head and double checking my arithmetic.
That's oversimplified.

It may be oversimplified but I have not added in some costs that I cannot calculate. Perhaps the Minister could have the officials of the Department of Health and Welfare do the calculations, and I invite him to do so. I think if he calculated the cost of the loss of interest on the money during the time it is paid out and paid back he would find there is an additional cost. He should add in as well the cost of hiring the extra tax police we will have to hire in Canada to administer the new taxation laws because here we are adding another 84
October 17, 1989

pages or so to the Income Tax Act of Canada, which is already enormous. Everybody knows the Income Thx Act is too complicated, except the Minister of Finance and the people advising him, who seem to make it more complicated with every passing year, and obviously his supporters on the back-bench who talk about the virtues of tax simplification and do everything they can to make it more incomprehensible and complicated.
I say that in all those circumstances the minister has done nothing to improve the tax law. He is going to have to hire more people and those additional persons are going to drive up the costs I have referred to of 17 cents on the dollar. It is going to go up, it is not going to go down and the ministers of this government are well aware of that fact.
I think those are reasons enough to consider rejecting this unfair tax but, as I said at the outset, every single one of the comments I have made in relation to old age security could be applied to the family allowances. Without having done the calculation, I would wager with any of the ministers present that the costs of administration of that program are higher because the amount of money dispensed under it is lower, and I am sure that more people, based on the dollars spent, are working in that particular branch or area of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
I think that the difficulties I have outlined with this tax and the difficulties I have outlined with this clawback provision, its unfairness, its meanness, its nastiness, and its inability to adjust to the changing circumstances of Canada's seniors in the 1990s, all dictate to us as members of parliament that we ought to reject this tax and vote against this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment my colleague from Kingston and the Islands for his usual analytical, logical and lucid discourse here in the House this afternoon.
I would like him to turn that analytical mind of his to the following comment that I have leading to, I hope, a question, because he was in fact dealing with the clawback. One of the interesting things in the clawback is the $50,000 limit. If we look at the analysis behind that we see, and many members have spoken on this, an inherent unfairness or discrimination in the treatment of
Government Orders
