Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak against Bill C-28. This bill does involve the clawback of old age security and of family allowance. It is an attack on the seniors of Canada and on the mothers of Canada.
I would first like to address the issue of the special tax on seniors. Fifty-eight per cent of Canadians over the age of 65 are women. These women, for the most part, belong to a generation characterized by low paid labour force participation and, therefore, low pension income. They have raised children and they have contributed over 40 years of valuable unpaid work to our society. Now the Conservative government is again attacking their pensions. The Tory government is saying to these women that their contributions over the years in building Canada, in making this country what it is, are not worthwhile.
I want to tell the Prime Minister that the contributions of which older women have made to this country are valuable. The last attack on seniors was the Prime Minister's attempt to de-index old age pensions. We saw then a powerful movement of seniors. They refused to give up their rights and they refused to be bled dry by this government. This proposed clawback of pensions is another angle that this government is taking to chip away at seniors' pension rights.
Although the government was not successful in de-indexing old age pensions, it did partially de-index family allowances in 1985. This bill constitutes another attack on the family allowance program in Canada. The government made family allowance worth less and less each year in terms of real spending power and now it will tax back what is left. It is just one of the many ways that this government is telling the women of Canada that bearing and raising children is not really important in our society.
It is amazing to me that on the one hand the government is almost attempting to force women to have children through threatened restrictions on abortion and recriminalization, through the slashing of family planning education, through the lack of commitment to research into safe and effective means of contraception, and on the other hand, it is taking away financial support from mothers who have children. Family allowance cheques are the only means of federal income support that goes specifically to mothers.
The universality of our carefully constructed social programs is in jeopardy. The old age security and family allowance programs are the victims of a free trade budget, one that seeks to harmonize our social programs with those of the United States. What we are now witnessing is the Americanization of our social programs and the end to universality.
We need to build a country in which the contributions of parents are recognized. We still live in a society in which women are expected to make personal sacrifices for their families. Women are far more likely to interrupt their paid work to take care of children. Close to 74 per cent of married women in a Statistics Canada survey cited family considerations as a reason for their first work interruption. Family considerations were a statistically negligible factor in the pattern of men's work interruptions. Women suffer financially for doing one of the most important jobs that there is in our society, that of raising the children. This government is making it more difficult for families with children to make ends meet. Women earn, on average, 66 per cent of what men earn in the paid labour force. Those with children need the supplementary income that the family allowance provides.
This government gives two arguments in favour of robbing seniors and mothers by plunging its greedy hands into the pockets of older people and children. I would like to deal with both of them. One argument is that we just cannot afford to treat people fairly. We just cannot afford universality, the Tories say. The Finance Minister sings his familiar tune about the deficit, about the strain on the public coffers. I ask the government why it is not taxing the large, profitable corporations in Canada that pay no tax rather than the seniors and the mothers of this country. I ask the government why it signed the free trade deal which is not only costing Canadians their jobs, but has also resulted in a loss of $2 billion in government revenues due to the lifting of tariffs.

WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT Mr. Vic Althouse (Mackenzie) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider
the advisability of introducing measures to amend the Western Grain
Stabilization Act to include coverage for producers who feed their
own grain to their livestock.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise today in private members' business to discuss a proposal which I have before the House as Motion No. 310, which asks the government to consider the advisability of introducing measures to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act to include coverage for producers who feed their own grain to their livestock.
The reasoning behind this is that I and many other Canadians in the agricultural business feel that there has been a form of discrimination in the way that we have formulated our stabilization laws over the past 30 or 40 years.
At the outset let me say that I had intended that this legislation would cover all of the stabilization acts in the country, but there was apparently a drafting error in that I had intended the motion to include not only Western Grain Stabilization Act but also the Agricultural Stabilization Act. Since I cannot amend my own motion, subsequent speakers, I presume, will be so doing. For purposes of my opening remarks, I would like to consider that both forms of stabilization program be included in the discussion.
I think that 40 and 50 years ago in Canada, agricultural economists and policy-makers seemed to be of the opinion-and this was the era when I was very young- that they had to provide policies that would encourage producers to focus on the production of a few items instead of the broad range of family farm production. There was a tendency among the bureaucrats and some of the politicians of the day to encourage the concentration of production into a few commodities.
Since that time, both the agricultural community and even some of the bureaucrats have noted that there are some problems going in this direction, because one can go too far. What we are left with is a series of policies that still encourage the production of single crops, or very few crops, and the encouragement of specialization into a very few commodities being produced on any one particular farm.
This has created some problems, both at the farm level and in rural communities, because by going too far in this direction we have ended up with programs like the Agricultural Stabilization Act and the Western Grain Stabilization Act, which presume that everyone should be producing grain for sale and not for secondary production on their own farms. In other words, they are

discouraging the secondary production at home and the adding of value to grain and forage production at the farm level.
The effects on the rural community have been quite noticeable. If we worked in a system that encouraged add-on and secondary production at the farm level, we would find that more people can be employed on fewer acres than is the case where you encouraged the specialization of grain production alone. Very few people on a great many acres is the result, and rural communities fade and die and, in fact, have disappeared on much of the prairies and other parts of Canada as well, but particularly on the prairies.
That has been encouraged in part by the view of stabilization that has been obtained since the early 1950s and which is reflected in the Agriculture Stabilization Act and in the Western Grain Stabilization Act. The result has been that we find some rather silly inequities.
During the past number of years there have been fairly large payouts under the Western Grain Stabilization Act and under the Agriculture Stabilization Act on grain because the grain market was very depressed. Those farmers who produced their grain for sale off the farm received relatively large subsidies to help offset the difference between the very low market price and their relatively high production costs. The result was that producers who were in grain only tended to get paid almost all of their production costs after the stabilization payments were received.
However, those producers who chose instead to feed all or part of their grain on the farm and engage in secondary production, which is good for the economy, better for the environment, and has a host of good social objectives tied to it, were in effect told by the signals from the law regarding stabilization payments that their type of production was no longer needed and was not appreciated. The effect was that they received less money for their grain production than their neighbour down the road.
There were ways around it that some enterprising individuals used. Some divided their cattle feeding, hog feeding, poultry or dairy operation from the grain producing sector and purchased it as a separate entity and made the grain production eligible thereby for stabilization payments. In general, people who fed their own
Private Members' Business
grain were feeding relatively high cost grain in competition with feeders who were buying grain at the market price which was lower cost to the feeder who was purchasing the grain. His costs were actually lower than the cost to the person who was growing his own under those conditions. That set up an unfair situation which I think government policy should not be encouraging to continue.
A number of organizations have pointed out the unfairness of this from the UPA in Quebec, I'Union des producteurs Agricoles, and the Canadian Pork Council which represents all of the provincial marketing boards across the country. I could go through the rather long list of organizations that have indicated that changes to these stabilization programs are needed, including the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, the Christian Farmers Federation of Ontario, the Ontario Cattlemen's Association, the Ontario Chicken Producers Marketing Board, the Ontario Egg Producers Marketing Board, the Ontario Milk Marketing Board, the Ontario Pork Producers Marketing Board, the Ontario Sheep Marketing Agency, and the Ontario Turkey Producers Marketing Board, just to mention the groups in Ontario. National groups include the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the National Farmers' Union; regional groups include the Prairie Pools Incorporated and others that I have already mentioned.
Various academics have looked at the question and have concluded that the stabilization payments should include farm-fed grain.
Daryl Kraft, an economist from the University of Manitoba, recommended that in his March, 1988 study of the Income Stabilization and Eligibility of Farm-fed Grain. One of the options under the Grains 2000 report included a farm-fed grain option being part of the stabilization program. Indeed, the need for farm-fed grain being included in stabilization programs is universal enough that there is no argument needed to convince legislators who make up this House as private members that it is needed.
The cost disadvantages have been quantified by various studies. Whether the study by Daryl Kraft is used, or

October 17, 1989
Private Members' Business
the study from the Ontario Park Producers Marketing Board, there are a variety of ranges of figures for the various commodities. Just to give you some idea of what sort of disadvantages this particular administration of the stabilization programs can produce, Mr. Speaker, I suggest you look at the figures provided by the Ontario Pork Producers Marketing Board. They estimated that producers who grow their own feed are at a disadvantage compared to producers who buy feed of about $6.30 per hog or 7.7 per cent of their cash costs. They state that the economics of the situation will dictate a move both away from land based operations and towards large integrators who buy their feed, or even to a movement of hog production completely out of the province. That is the problem.
A similar distortion exists in the poultry industry, in the dairy industry, and in the beef industry. It is there. I will not go on boring you with a series of numbers, Mr. Speaker, I have some that would show that in the cattle industry the losses per head are much larger than with pork.
The only thing that has held back legislators and administrators up to this point was that previous to three or four years ago they could not see any workable way of administering this kind of a program. I submit that there are now several provinces that have been experimenting with programs to pay producers under slightly different programs. The administrative procedures that they have come up with would work in administering the stabilization acts that I mentioned in my remarks.
The province of Alberta has provided a system whereby it has attempted to pay the so-called Crow benefit to producers. I do not agree with the payment of that benefit as a matter of policy, but Alberta has created an administrative procedure which is possible to copy. It has simply computed the conversion factors for grains into beef, into litres of milk, into dozens of eggs, into pounds of poultry meat and decided that if the farm can show that it has produced x number of pounds of production of those commodities it will simply apply a mathematical formula to that and arrive at a presumption of how much farm-fed grain must have been consumed on that farm in order to have that level of production. It deducts any feed purchases from that and the difference is a farm-fed grain. The subsidy is paid on the basis of the tonnes of grain that are produced from that formula.
The formula is there. The administration has been tried in Alberta and is now being copied under similar programs in Saskatchewan and in Manitoba. That formula could be applied under the Agricultural Stabilization Act and under the Western Grain Stabilization Act to provide a payment for farm-fed grains, with the result that there would be no discouragement on the part of government programs. There would no longer be discrimination against those producers who chose to feed livestock, or poultry, or dairy cattle on the farm. It would stop being an impediment to the continuation of secondary production at the farm level. It would permit those communities where the individuals so wish to engage in value-added production at the farm and in their own communities.
This has good implications for the social fabric of those rural communities, and also for the total environment for all of us, because it would tend to disperse livestock production, making not only the accompanying smells easier to deal with, but the accompanying by-products and manure easier to dispose of and more available and useful to the soil for incorporation to continue the production cycle.
It has the advantage of being acceptable in a social context, in an environmental context, and I believe, since it has all these things going for it, that it is also high time that it was acceptable in a political context. The House, as private members, should approve the motion as it should be amended and recommend it for immediate action to the government.

Mr. Speaker, Canada's grain industry has been faced with a number of economic pressures in recent years. World grain subsidy battles, heavy debt loads, and drought have created hardships for agriculture and rural Canada. The agricultural trade environment is changing rapidly. In dealing with these facts, we have relied to a large extent on ad hoc government support programs. Farmers clearly need the assistance to improve their long-term financial stability.
Farmers across the country agree, as well, that there has to be a better way than the ad hoc methods that we have fallen back on over the last few years. There is also a general agreement that whatever we do, it must be

Private Members' Business
consistent with our international efforts to reform agricultural subsidies.
In recent years support programs have paid out very large amounts. Crop insurance payments last year were close to $1 billion. The Special Canadian Grains Program paid $2.1 billion in two years to offset low grain prices brought on by those international subsidy wars. Payments under the Special Canadian Grains Program were made on a wide variety of crops, and farm-fed grain was included.
This year, the Canadian crop drought assistance program paid out $850 million to help farmers who suffered drought losses in 1988. We have in that drought program a graphic illustration that no matter how you design an emergency program, there will be perceived inadequacies and cries of unfairness. The administrators of ad hoc programs have to develop artificial criteria, criteria outside of the market-place and, therefore, unreal. They have to draw lines. Some individuals find themselves on the wrong -side of the line. If the lines are moved, adjusted, or redrawn, there are still an equal number of people who find themselves on the wrong side of the line who may harbour feelings of unfairness.
Ad hoc programs, like special grains 1 and 2 and the crop drought assistance program, as well as the contributory programs, like crop insurance and WGSA, have delivered huge sums of money which have helped to keep the prairie grain sector afloat over the past several years. Indeed, the recent Economic Council of Canada report, which is entitled "Canadian Prairie Farming, 1960-2000" at page 8 states:
In the wake of the sharp decline in world grain prices and of the international grain price war, the Canadian government provided additional support to prairie farmers. In 1987, direct payments under the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Special Canadian Grains Program amounted to $2.2 billion, or roughly $17,000 per prairie farmer. Direct and indirect payments under numerous other federal and provincial farm programs added roughly another $1.8 billion, bringing the total up to $4 billion, or about $31,000 per farmer. Thus, during the most recent years, government support accounted for nearly all of the net farm income on prairie farms.
There is no question that that historic level of support was entirely justified. One would hate to imagine the state of rural Canada without those programs.
The fact is that emergency programs cannot possibly be fine Tuned down to the point where they are deemed to be absolutely fair for every single producer. It is simply not possible to reach perfect fairness and equity between individuals under ad hockery, any more than it is possible to have perfect fairness and equity between producers in-sofar as the effects of weather or climate are concerned.
The bottom line is that we must develop better long-term programs for Canadian agriculture, programs like enhanced crop insurance, programs like a contributory income assurance plan so that participating producers can exercise some independence of judgment and tailor safety net programs to suit their own needs, programs that work so that ad hoc, emergency type programs will not be needed in the future. That is the desire of this government and of the farm community generally. We look forward, with anticipation, to seeing the results of the current agricultural policy review.
The issue we are discussing today, inclusion of farm-fed grain in the western grain stabilization program, is not new. Western Canadians have argued that farm-fed grain should be included. The western grain stabilization program provides protection to farmers based on the amount of grain they sell. If they feed their grain on their own farm, they do not have the eligible grain sales necessary to contribute levies to WGS and ultimately to receive payments. This inequity is a major cause of concern to farmers. Large payments through the program in recent years have heightened awareness of the situation. Farmers in other parts of the country want changes too. For instance, maritime farmers who feed a major portion of the grain they produce to livestock want stabilization; so do Quebec and Ontario producers.
The matter of inclusion of farm-fed grains was discussed by the agriculture committee of this House in January of 1986. In the report that was filed by that committee, farm-fed grain was considered and this statement was made:
It should be only for the final products marketed that the producer receives market risk protection under the WGSA or the ASA. In the case of livestock producers, they face the livestock market but not the grain market risk. Treating livestock producers as grain producers means the grain may be covered in the raw form and again as it goes into the final product.

There was mention of a possible double benefit, depending on conditions. There was also mention made by the committee benefit and, of course, of verification of sales, to say nothing of the cost. The recommendation at that time was that undesignated sales remain ineligible under the WGSA.
Nonetheless, with farmers in all agricultural regions of the country asking for change, it is clear that a broad look has to be given to this issue. That is exactly what is being done. A major review of grain income stabilization began over a year ago. This review is examining options for a national stabilization program for all farmers. It is an attempt to treat all farmers in an equitable way.
The review process began in the summer of 1988, when representatives of government met with farm leaders in all regions. Through these meetings, government was provided with guidelines which were used to develop options for a new stabilization scheme. A number of options for stabilization were subsequently developed by Agriculture Canada's national grains bureau in Winnipeg. These options were presented to farm leaders who met again in Winnipeg last January. The farm leaders indicated they would continue to discuss options for grain stabilization with their members.
One message that came through clearly in these meetings was that the farm groups favour a national approach to grain stabilization. They want that approach to be as fair as possible to all producers, and they want the issues of eligibility and production neutrality addressed. The process has been productive and it continues.
In the meantime it should be understood that this government has already taken some steps to provide better income stabilization for farmers. Of course, further reforms are being looked at, but I think we should outline the progress that has been made. This government, back in 1984, made a commitment to improve the WGSA and that commitment was met. In February of 1985, the act was amended to allow for timely interim payments to be made before the end of the crop year, in time to assist farmers with their spring seeding expenses. Since the amendment, interim payments totalling about $2.4 billion have been made.
Significant improvements were also made to the WGSA in 1988, amendments designed to encourage greater participation in the program and to put it on firm financial ground. These included a $750 million federal write-down of the WGSA's deficit. Without this writedown, the future of the program was in doubt. Nine crops were added to the list of crops eligible for contribution. Amendments also raised levies in the jointly funded program. Tb encourage more farmers to join, a 10 per cent penalty for rejoining producers was removed.
These changes to WGSA were made as part of this government's strategy to strengthen and improve the safety net system for grain farmers.
We are currently involved in a review of every facet of Canadian agricultural policy. Grain stabilization is just one area that this government is looking at with a view to the future.
In closing, I want to commend the member for Mackenzie for again raising the matter of farm-fed grains. It is an old problem but one that ought not to be overlooked. It is a difficult problem. It is being examined and hopefully can be addressed in the over-all policy.
Finally, I want to say a word about Bill C-36, the advance payment for stored grains legislation. We all know that Canada faces a very difficult national debt problem and the interest payments to service that debt, created by past governments, are choking the ability of governments today to be able to deliver the programs that farmers need. In order to cope with that deficit, an interest payment problem, all departments of government were asked in the budget this spring to make some sacrifice in the national interest. One of the things that agriculture was asked to give up was the interest fee provision for advance payments.
Many of my constituents are now telling me that they recognize the fact that the budgetary decision had to be made. Some may not like it but they do understand it. What they cannot now understand is the failure of this House of Commons to effect speedy passage of Bill C-36 in order that cash advances can be drawn.
This government is ready, willing and able to effect speedy passage of Bill C-36.1 urge my fellow members and colleagues to support speedy passage in order that

those farmers who wish to take out cash advances on farm stored grain can do so.
It seems to me at this point that the stalling of that legislation, for whatever reason, partisan or otherwise, is not in the best interest of producers. I urge my hon. colleagues to co-operate with this government and with the farm community in this regard by co-operating in regard to Bill C-36.

What we are seeing, for example, in the free trade legislation, is one measure after another by the Americans to undercut the family farm. We see the pork producers in western Canada under tremendous strain. We see that the provincial government of

Alberta has had to bail out one producer while another producer in another community was laying off people.

There was an article in The Winnipeg Free Press recently about the stress on the family farm. For example, as the push comes on the farmer from the bank, from the lack of price support and so forth, at least one person if not both people are forced from their farm to take part-time work. In rural areas in western Canada women in particular are being forced to leave their traditional roles, sometimes against their will, to take on other roles in the community. I think that should be studied by the House. I hope that the agricultural committee will take on some initiative in assessing just how the family farm is being pushed around by this government.
The stress is also felt by the very fact that so many western Canadians spend their winters and their falls undertaking special seminars. For example, next week in Brandon, Manitoba, for the second time, the weekly newspapers across Manitoba are sponsoring a seminar to

October 17, 1989
Private Members' Business
talk about stresses on farms to see what they can do to change the present regime.
Our party supports the motion, as I stated at the outset, but there is some difficulty. Perhaps, if the government had listened to the opposition back when it was discussed in the agriculture committee in 1986 as the previous member stated, we would have been able to come to some agreement on how to best monitor the farm-fed issue.
We must set up some regulatory regime which does not overwhelm the farmer but somehow sets out a control mechanism so farmers can begin to act more independently while there is a true costing arrangement and a true stabilization process involved that does not cause the government to have to expand its workforce or cause farming families to have to increase their paper load.
It is not clear from the motion that its movers understand fully just how complicated it is from this point of view. I can only hope that as this debate continues through the House in the coming months we will be able to clarify the best ways of helping the farmers out on this particular issue.
Farm-fed grains are currently not included under the Western Grain Stabilization Act. The Grains 2000 study which this government is supposedly using to formulate agricultural policy in this area has recommended that farm-fed grain be included under the Western Grain Stabilization Act. Those policy makers who are examining the move to a tripartite system for crop insurance and income stabilization programs feel that farm-fed grains should come under the act. Mixed farmers would certainly appreciate a little help as they try to deal with the economic hardship caused for the most part by the misguided economic and agricultural policies of this government.
By adopting this motion we will create the opportunity to help mixed farmers with their immediate problem. By allowing them to receive a benefit for farm-fed grain, they will be able to keep their herds at a level that is dictated by a market need instead of a financial crisis which they are all in. The reality is that there will be no help coming from the Progressive Conservative government and its Prime Minister.
In particular, I hold responsible the Deputy Prime Minister who should know better, given his criticism of governments dating back to the mid-1970s. The Western Grain Stabilization Act no longer serves the western grain economy. Its only reason for existing is to serve the crass political manoeuvring of a government known for its intellectual corruption as much as for its lack of compassion.
So far this year there has been no payment from the Western Grain Stabilization Act. It is unlikely that there will be any payments later this year. Last year, before the election, the western grain stabilization program made record payouts to farmers. When we consider how the government this year is claiming to be so cash short, it is odd to remember just how easily it was able to find moneys last year, whether we are talking about this particular piece of legislation or the western diversification fund. After the election, it was discovered, lo and behold, that the government used the wrong formula and overpaid the farmers who received benefits from the program. Surprise, surprise.
The government sent out notices telling the farmers that they had to pay back all the excess funds. This is the new Tory philosophy: they do not have to buy votes; they only have to rent them.
This government must come to its senses: stop playing the cat and mouse game with farmers and start coming up with policies that will help strengthen our farm sector. In this vein we support the motion.

Mr. Speaker, indeed it is a pleasure to stand in the House and actually whole-heartedly endorse and support the motion by the hon. member for Mackenzie, my colleague from Saskatchewan.
I was not quite sure, in listening to the remarks from the member for Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assini-boia speaking on behalf of the government, whether in fact government members intended to support this particular motion. I got the distinct impression that they were not going to and find that very disappointing.
Not only did I find his remarks disappointing in that he implied there would not be support coming from the government, I was also disappointed that he never dealt with the substance of the hon. member's motion. Rather, he dragged red herrings across the trail of the debate by dealing with issues like the drought payment, trying to cover up the government's poor track record with re-
October 17, 1989

spect to that program, and dragging out again the issue of the advance payments.
As farmers very well know, it was 152 days from the time the government did not provide the money in the budget to cover those payments until it introduced an acceptable bill. Since then the opposition has been debating for about 20 hours. I found it very unfortunate that the member tried to use that particular argument in the context of this debate.
What I really found unfortunate is that it appeared that the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia at a very fundamental level did not understand what the hon. member for Mackenzie in fact was saying, that the livestock producer who uses farm-fed grain is discriminated against under the present system. The member for Swift Current-Maple Creek- Assiniboia implied that while the producer of farm-fed grain might not be covered under the grain stabilization program, that farmer, however, would then become eligible for coverage under the livestock stabilization program to compensate for that.
That is not the case because the livestock stabilization program uses the market value of that grain in computing the formulas on which the payouts under the program are based. The problem is that the market value does not include the value that people who are eligible for stabilization get from the grain stabilization program. The amount that people get under grain stabilization is not part of that market price. Therefore it does not get figured into the formula to arrive at the payout levels of the livestock stabilization program. I think it is a very clear case of livestock producers who feed their own grain being discriminated against.
It is very unfortunate that the member perhaps has based the opposition of the government to this particular motion on something that is not even factual and a complete misunderstanding of the situation.
The second argument that the member used was that as a result of some past discussions on the subject it has been deemed to be administratively difficult or impossible to arrive at a fair formula for a fairer system for administering the inclusion of farm-fed grains. Again, the member could not have been listening to the hon. member for Mackenzie, because he explained in some detail how the government of Alberta, followed now by
Private Members' Business
the governments of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, in fact has evolved a very workable system to incorporate the veiy features into provincial programs that he is calling for at the federal level to be included in the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act.
I think the member for Mackenzie dealt very well with the question of administration. It always seems a little ironic to me that we are dealing with a situation where I understand there are 400 planners in the Department of Agriculture. I am not saying those people do not do good work or that they are not good people. I presume they are.
There are 400 planners in that department, and it always seems a little ironic to me that something that can be understood by most farmers, and was eloquently outlined here by the member for Mackenzie, should be something that 400 planners cannot manage to incorporate into a government program.
I guess those are the same 400 planners who are holding jobs that probably pay $30,000, $40,000, or $50,000 a year and who shortly are going to release a document on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture saying that farmers should be less dependent on government handouts. When you consider the source of that kind of wisdom you sometimes must wonder about the equity of what we are dealing with.
The other point that the member for Swift Current- Maple Creek-Assiniboia raised in suggesting that perhaps he would not be supporting this legislation was that somehow or other it ran afoul of international trade laws and that since we are having so many problems in other areas perhaps this would simply compound that.
I think that is really unfortunate because the grain stabilization bill and the Agricultural Stabilization Act are specifically dealt with I believe in the free trade agreement with the United States and, as well, are fully concurrent with the GATT regime.
Therefore to enhance the agriculture industry through this particular measure would in fact be utilizing a mechanism that is recognized in the international community and would show some leadership in the international field by developing a way to support integrated

October 17, 1989
Private Members' Business
farming operations through a support program which does not distort trade in the international arena.
I hope we have not heard the last word on the intentions of members opposite because I would veiy much like to plead with them to support this particular initiative. I think the member for Mackenzie has introduced many good ideas on agricultural programs into the House through the years. I think his contribution here needs to be recognized for giving leadership not necessarily on a partisan basis but for offering a very progressive and forward looking perspective on agricultural questions. I think he is respected by farm organizations from coast to coast, as well as by members opposite. It seems to me that on something that makes as much sense as this it only seems right to support the hon. member.
This is a votable motion with five hours of debate. One of the objectives of introducing that kind of system into this House, the private members' system, is to allow private members some input into the general direction of government policy, the policy if you will of this House. Even though we are engaging in a major agricultural review at this time, I think this would be a clear direction from all sides in this House that this is a direction in which we would like to see agriculture go in this country.
I would also like to indicate briefly a few of my own reasons for supporting this motion. I agree with the hon. member that the whole trend toward specialization as opposed to mixed farming is in many ways a dead end. It is a dead end socially. It is a dead end environmentally. It is a dead end economically. I think that is becoming more and more evident to more and more farmers, certainly to policy makers and to the public at large.
I think we have to do everything we can to maintain the family size unit, the average size farm, the smaller farm in this country. We are losing farmers so fast it is getting hard to count them.
We look at alarming statistics such as in our own province of Saskatchewan where they say that the average farm is about 1,000 acres. However, those statistics do not say that only 14,000 farms are 1,000 acres or bigger, while 39,000 farms are under 1,000 acres in size. That means there are only 14,000 farms which are
considered to be commercially viable, while 39,000 farms are vulnerable if they are based entirely on grain production. In our province we are experiencing not only farm loss but a general population loss.
I think this kind of initiative is most timely but in fact might well be too late for a lot of people. I think as well that when the government talks about sustainable agriculture it behoves us to start looking at these kinds of initiatives very seriously. We are obviously mining our soil at a rate that we cannot maintain, and we cannot close our eyes to this situation forever.
I have farmed for the last 14 years, and family and neighbours farm as well. Short-term economics have been pressing in on us and probably causing us to adopt some practices we would rather not accept, but I would certainly like to see us take seriously the whole issue of soil conservation, of stewardship of the land and of our resources.
Having said that, I would like in closing to move the amendment that the hon. member intended to be a part of this bill but which through the drafting did not appear. I move:
That the motion be amended by adding after the words "Western
Grain Stabilization Act" the following:
and Agricultural Stabilization Act.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: On debate, the hon. parliamentary secretary.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by expressing my gratitude for the opportunity to participate today and by saying that I very much enjoyed the time which I was able to spend on the Standing Committee on Agriculture with the hon. member for Mackenzie. I always found his contribution in committee to be thought provoking and invaluable. Certainly I listened with care to his remarks again today and found them to be equally enjoyable.
I am also pleased to note the amendment which has just been moved, Mr. Speaker, because I think, as all of us in this House understand, it is exceedingly important that issues such as farm-fed grain be addressed on a national basis. There are unfortunately so many problems in agriculture today that to try to address them on a
October 17, 1989

regional basis would not do justice to the nature of the motion before the House. I believe the amendment which has been moved is certainly an appropriate one. I would have been distressed had the proposal been only to look at the western Canadian stabilization program and not the Agricultural Stabilization Act.
Mr. Speaker, as I think you know, the whole issue of farm-fed grain is one of many of considerable importance which is currently being addressed by the federal government and its representatives in co-operation with provincial governments and with farm leaders throughout the country. There have been a number of meetings, the objective of which is to tiy to add to the degree of stability which unfortunately is not always present in agriculture. Quite clearly it has not been present in the last two or three years.
I have looked forward with some anticipation to the results of those meetings because, although I am very proud as a member of this government of the amount of financial assistance which we have been able to provide to Canadian agriculture since 1984-and I think most people in this House who remember understand that there has been a record amount of such financial assistance-I continue to be frustrated and troubled by the fact that ad hoc programs are never fully adequate for the needs of those who are participants in them.
Unfortunately it is virtually impossible to devise ad hoc programs in such a way that they are always equitable or at least perceived to be equitable. Certainly, without doubt, while the drought program for 1988 is providing a much needed $850 million to Canadian farm producers, it has created a great amount of administrative difficulty due to the fact that we are dealing in many cases with inadequate documentation of crop reduction.
I truly hope that one of the results of the meetings which have been taking place in the last few months will be fewer programs in agriculture, less dependence on ad hoc programs, and that with the type of insurance programs in place the farm community will be able to determine well in advance what its rights are and what the level of protection will be, much in the same way that an urban resident is able to take out fire insurance on a house or something of that nature. We need that kind of stability.
Private Members' Business
There is no question that there is a difficulty within the western grain stabilization program and with agricultural stabilization at the moment in that people who do feed grain on the farm-and that is some 30 per cent of all grain production in the country or about one-half of the cereals if you exclude wheat from that calculation-are not eligible to participate in the western grain stabilization program, to use that as an example.
Consequently there is a feeling of frustration and unfortunately what happens is that very often farmers reorganize their business so that in a sense there will be two businesses. They split their operations so that family members in one case can produce grain and sell it to another family member in order to enhance their likelihood of being able to participate in the western grain stabilization program. That has been a problem and continues to be a problem. I know it is one of the areas of concern of those who participate in those meetings to which I have already referred and which they will certainly be addressing.
The difficulty with this program is not unique to western Canada. The concerns are there in the mari-times and other parts of Canada as well.
However, finding a solution to this problem is not simply a matter of adding farm-fed grain to the stabilization programs, whether it be the Western Grain Stabilization Act or the Agricultural Stabilization Act. In fact, in so doing we might be in some danger of creating another set of inequities to replace those which are currently there.
For example, some dairy producers already have the cost of producing grain built into their milk prices. To make such grain eligible for grain stabilization payments as well could amount to duplication and of course would be inequitable to other producers.
The main motion deals specifically with the idea of including farm-fed grain in the western grain stabilization program. I think there are two or three points that need to be addressed, because it certainly is something that the committee on which I had the honour to serve as chairman back in 1986 spent a lot of time addressing. As a previous colleague has already indicated, however, we were not able to resolve some of the problems which were then before us.

Private Members' Business
For example, to include farm-fed grain in the Western Grain Stabilization Act would require a fundamental change, and that is a change in the basic structure of the program itself. The WGSA, as most members of this House know, would have to then become a production based program rather than a program based on recognized commercial grain sales.
As already indicated this would present its own set of issues. For instance, the collection of good yield data would be essential to a production based program. Certainly the need for that yield data is there, but it is readily apparent from the drought program that crop insurance statistics by themselves are not sufficient to provide that data.
Unless a reliable set of individual yield histories were available, stabilization payments might then have to be based on regional yield averages. One of the problems with those averages is that there are differences. There are inequities. Producers with yields below the regional average would be overcompensated, while the other half of the farmers with production statistics above the average would be penalized. Also, such a program could result in payouts at a time when livestock returns are adequate or even at a peak.
Changing the WGSA into a production based program would also remove the protection that farmers now have from reduced marketings because of reduced export opportunities. Currently, if delivery opportunities are reduced, lower marketings can result and the lower net cash flow can then trigger payments under WGSA. If WGSA were to become production based it would not respond as readily to fluctuations in marketings.
Aside from these considerations it must also be understood that including farm-fed grain in WGSA would add to the cost of the program, This is a program to which the farmer contributes as well as the federal government. That would add to the farmer's cost at a time when, as we all know too well, cash flow is far less than adequate particularly in western Canada.
Unfortunately crops in my own constituency of Brandon-Souris are worse even in 1989 than they were in 1988. Consequently we are not in a position to be able to afford additional payments at this time.
Other options have been discussed from time to time that I think are important and should be noted. Some have suggested including the cost of grain production in livestock stabilization programs. At the present time livestock price support typically includes the market price of grain and calculations to determine support but not the cost of producing the grain.
Dairy support programs include grain production costs to a degree. Support calculations which include the cost of grain production would result in higher livestock support prices when costs of producing grain increase. This could provide an incentive to farmers to produce both grain and livestock to be eligible for grain stabilization programs. However, it would work against producers who buy feed for their livestock.
Another option which has been considered is jointly stabilizing grain and livestock revenues by stabilizing combined net revenue from the two enterprises. This type of program would have to be operated at the farm level in order to take into account differences in the importance of each enterprise. In the case of a mixed farm operation where the returns are more stable, lower levy rates could be applied.
The government is currently examining options for grain safety net programs and I look forward to that. Farmers involved in the review process agree that this issue must be dealt with on a national scale. Inclusion of farm-fed grain in stabilization programs was, in fact, one of the issues reviewed by the Standing Committee on Agriculture, as we have already noted. This was also raised in meetings with farm leaders last year and again during the course of the last few months.
This review, which is currently under way, will be looking at many issues other than just farm-fed grain. I do hope that one of the results of the review will be the creation of a comprehensive safety net program of which, I would assume, the Western Grain Stabilization Act may be a part. I would assume that crop insurance and the red meat stabilization programs, of which I think we are appropriately proud, would be a part as well.
In reviewing all of these programs, I hope that the House would agree that it is important in the end to try to include each of the areas of deficiency that we have identified-and farm-fed grain is only one of many-so that the final result of these meetings with the farm leaders and with the provinces will be a type of comprehensive farm insurance program in which farmers can ensure from year to year that they have a relatively stable income and that their incomes will not be subject
October 17, 1989

to the fluctuations in marketing and prices as it has been in the past. And, if it is possible to include farm-fed grain as part of that package, then certainly I think all members of the House would agree that that would be a worthy objective as well.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Before I call upon the hon. member for Red Deer, I have examined the amendment and, although I have some reservation, I will give the hon. member the benefit of the doubt and we will accept the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity this evening to respond to the private member's motion on inclusion of farm-fed grain in the western grain stabilization program. Before I begin my speech, Mr. Speaker, may I ask you a question? In light of the hour on the clock, will I have an opportunity to continue my remarks later, or should I talk very rapidly at this point?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member will have nine minutes remaining in his speech when we finish at six o'clock. If he does not hurry, he will lose that.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. In my opinion, there are a number of reasons why including farm-fed grain in the western grain stabilization program is not practical. I would like to outline some of those reasons for you.
First of all, the amendment you have just accepted is an improvement over the original motion. The Western Grain Stabilization Act is a program which applies only to farmers in the Canadian Wheat Board designated areas of western Canada. Grain stabilization concerns farmers in all regions of Canada and if we look, as the original motion did, at one region only, it would not be in the best interests of producers because it would address the issue in too narrow a context.
I still have a very real concern that by adding farm-fed grain to the Western Grain Stabilization Act, we would perhaps be creating more inequities than those that already exist. This proposed change to the Western
Adjournment Debate
Grain Stabilization Act would involve a major, fundamental change to the program. Including farm-fed grain in the western grain stabilization program would mean changing the basic structure of the program.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the House of Commons some time ago, I raised the issue with the government about VIA Rail and the cut-backs that were forced upon the constituency that I have the honour and privilege to represent.
The government has shut down 40 per cent of the rail lines between Ottawa and Montreal. It has also shut down 25 per cent of the lines between Ottawa and Toronto. Many people in the constituency that I represent use VIA Rail to go to work. They use it to commute between Alexandria and Montreal, and elsewhere. I feel that it is unfair that these people are now being deprived of this essential service.
The government says that it cannot afford VIA Rail any more. Why could it so much afford it during the election campaign? Why was the Prime Minister, during the election campaign, standing on a train platform in Actonvale, Quebec, saying to the people of that part of the country that VIA Rail was there to stay and that the Prime Minister had seen to it that train service was restored?

October 17, 1989
Adjournment Debate
The Financial Post of September 14,1989 identified one of the reasons why VIA Rail is in the present deficit situation. It talks about the fact that CN Rail is recording a profit and VIA Rail is recording a loss. Both are Crown corporations and one corporation is dependent on the other for the use of its track. It says:
In CN's case this is particularly galling, since the railway claims to be operating at a profit - "a business as well as a responsibility" is one of its slogans. Yet on closer examination it will be seen that for most of its life span VIA, has been one of CN's top two customers, the other being grain transport which is also heavily subsidized.
What we have, then, is a hat-and-shell game in which one public corporation, claiming a profit, is dependent on another which runs at a loss.
The problem now appears to be that my constituents are losing a service because CN Rail and CP Rail in some measure charge much too much for that track fee.
I had another problem in the constituency that I represent in regard to rail transport. It is the fact that the residents of my province commute to Montreal using passenger train. The government member who will be charged with responding to this will say, "Yes, but commuter rail is the responsibility of the province." I disagree.
Which province is going to be responsible for taking commuters from Alexandria, Ontario, to Montreal, Quebec, the Government of Ontario, when 90 per cent of the track is located in Quebec, or the Government of Quebec taking Ontarians to work in another province? Both, of course, are going to claim that it is not their responsibility and that the responsibility belongs elsewhere.

Mr. Speaker, it is clear the Government must help provide transportation for passengers who travel from one province to another to go to work. In fact, a precedent has already been set by the fact that the National Capital Commission annually pays $974,000 to the Outaouais Regional Community Transit Commission and $608,000 to the Ottawa-Carleton Regional Transit Commission.
These subsidies by the NCC, a federal government agency, acknowledge the need for passengers to commute from one province to another to get to work.
Mr. Speaker, I say to the Conservative Government that the Minister is not on track on this issue. It is high time the Government remembered that Canadians want to keep their railways and want to keep VIA Rail.

I say to the government that this plan should be derailed and should be derailed immediately. The minister has told us that we are going to have a royal commission of inquiry to study whether or not we should have shut down VIA Rail when we already did. I say that that is putting the caboose before the engine.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has made mention of what we campaigned on last year during the election campaign. I would like to tell him that we did promise Canadians during the election campaign that we would take responsibility for fiscal management of the affairs of Canada. I feel that the action we have taken in this last couple of weeks is a very position step in that direction.
I would like to offer to the hon. member some views on the government's decision on VIA's five-year corporate plan. The government's decision maintains a national, affordable, sustainable network of all rail passenger services, while at the same time being financially responsible. We do not have unlimited resources from the general treasury to pour into rail passenger service.
The government determined that Canadian taxpayers can simply no longer afford to spend so much on VIA when it offers such a low return on the ridership and revenues. VIA's ridership has dropped by 20 per cent since 1981. Its cost recovery continues to hover around 30 per cent. The corporation required an unprecedented $641 million in subsidies in 1988 alone, or an average of $100 for every person who boarded the train.
The government had to act, and having decided on VIA's corporate plan, chose to use the powers of the Governor in Council to act quickly. Delay would have cost the Canadian taxpayers further millions of dollars which, quite frankly, we cannot afford. The decision was not taken lightly and was taken only after careful deliberation and consideration of the representations received from individual Canadians, provincial ministers, mayors and other representatives of municipalities and
October 17, 1989

numerous other groups. Close attention was paid to all other concerns and suggestions.
The national network that we envisage strikes the best balance between the real transportation needs of Canada and its fiscal realities.

Mr. Speaker, I asked the Minister of Transport what I feel is a very important question and that is, following the cancellation of VIA service in eastern Nova Scotia between Truro and Sydney, was it not natural to assume that freight service would follow, and that the rail would be abandoned. The minister stated that this was not so much a question for him or for the government but for the NTA, that the NTA, under the National Transportation Act, had jurisdiction in deciding what rail lines were to be abandoned. He completely neglected to give me an unequivocal promise that that rail line would not be abandoned.
The minister, by not giving an unequivocal answer, has abandoned his responsibility as Minister of Transport to maintain a comprehensive transportation policy in this country. It is very important that areas such as mine know what the government is going to do, regardless of whether it is the responsibility of the National Transportation Act or not. It is the government's responsibility to maintain the services.
It is vital because many people in this country presume that because rail passenger service has been cancelled, rail freight service is to follow and those that lost passenger service will lose rail service completely and those rail lines will be abandoned. In Cape Breton, which needs industry badly, we are now facing the prospect of prospective investors saying there is not going to be a railroad that because there is no passenger service, ultimately it is only a matter of time before there is not going to be freight service. The minister would not state to the contrary.
It is made additionally difficult because the government appointed the president of CN to be president of VIA and asked that president of VIA, who was also president of CN, to do a study as to the rail feasibility for passenger lines in Canada. He decided which lines were to be closed and that recommendation was then given to the government. The president of VIA, by closing the VIA service in many parts of Canada, helped to make his
Adjournment Debate
case as president of CN for the abandonment of those particular lines. It is just not acceptable.
Also, unless we get an unequivocal statement from the government that rail lines in this country are going to be kept open, then we are inviting CN to downgrade the service to help them make its case for that particular rail abandonment. It has been done in other areas. It has been brought up at hearings that CN will intentionally reduce the service to make that service look as bad as possible to make its case for rail abandonment. It does not want many rail lines in Atlantic Canada, if it wants any rail lines at all. We cannot give it that opportunity. It is important that the government says that rail lines in eastern Nova Scotia will not be abandoned, that the service from Halifax to Sydney will continue. Then we will have CN making the best of that line, making as economic use as possible of that line, and maintaining that line.
CN has already entered into an arrangement to ship containers from Halifax to St. John's directly, thereby cutting down the container traffic from North Sydney to Newfoundland by 75 per cent, thereby starting to make its case. It buys rails from Sydney Steel Corporation. Imagine buying rails from a steel plant that may not have a railroad to ship those rails out on. Some people say, well, you can ship them by water. If you could ship them by water as cheaply as CN can on its track, then of course we would have done it before. But, of course, it uses those rails at intermittent spots across the country. Shipping to one particular location means extra handling and extra costs for it.
We have coal shipments in Cape Breton to clients whom we badly need to maintain a very struggling economy. Each coal car contains 100 tonnes. For each coal car, we would need four eighteen-wheel trucks to carry that same amount of coal. One of my constituents counted at a crossing 54 coal cars. That would mean 216 18-wheel trucks on the highways. Imagine what that would do to the tourist industry when the train goes through the centre of the island without much recognition whatsoever?
It is important that that rail line be maintained in Cape Breton and eastern Nova Scotia. It is vital that the government make a commitment and recognize the importance of maintaining that rail line. There should be no more backsliding. There cannot be any more dillydallying on the part of the government. We must draw the line for Canada and say to the people of Cape Breton and eastern Nova Scotia that the government is the

October 17, 1989
Adjournment Debate
government of all of Canada and not just of the areas that are numerous in population. There is a Canada outside the main metropolitan areas. It is important that this government recognize that.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys has raised concerns regarding the possible branch line abandonment that the government has announced in its plan for the restructured rail passenger network. I can appreciate the concerns that he has raised here today and on other occasions. I also want to assure him that the government appreciates the concerns because we have to represent all areas of the country.
As the Blouse knows, it is for the National Transportation Agency to rule on the requests for branch line abandonment for CN and CP which are currently before the agency. They have to give due notice of their intentions.
The National Transportation Act of 1987 lays out the matters at which the agency must look in making its decision. The act does not call in any way for a line to be abandoned just because VIA Rail is no longer using the line.
I would remind members that in the fall of last year, the Minister of Transport asked the National Transportation Agency to seek the views of the provinces with regard to the criteria that it should be using for branch line abandonment and its concept of a basic rail network. I can assure the House that all proposals for branch line abandonment will be considered very carefully as the law requires.
The hon. member has also made the implication in his remarks that the president of CN, in functioning as VIAs chief executive officer, might have conflicting objectives in respect to branch line abandonment. I can assure him that this is not the case. In hearings today before the transport committee, we heard that it is a very small portion of CN's revenue that comes by way of VIA Rail. There is that myth that a large portion of its
revenue is from VIA. That is not the case. He gave the figures before the committee today.
In either his capacity as President of CN or as the chief executive officer of VIA or CN, the ownership of the rail line is not an issue in the government's decision to maintain a sustainable and an affordable national rail transportation network.
ALBERTA BUSINESS LOANS PORTFOLIO/REVERSAL OF POLICY-POSITION OF THE MINISTER

Mr. Speaker, on June 16 of this year, I put a question to the hon. Minister of Finance, concerning business loans by the chartered banks in Alberta. At that time, I noted that business loans by Canada's chartered banks had declined by 50 per cent in Alberta from 1982 to 1988. They dropped from an annual average of $18.1 billion in 1982 to $9.1 billion in 1988.1 noted as well that given average dollars invested per new job created figures for Alberta, that collapse of bank business financing in Alberta cost the people of that province somewhere between 100,000 and 140,000 jobs.
Two related elements make this abandoning of Alberta businesses by Canada's chartered banks all the more strange. First, indigenous financial institutions in Alberta actually increased their assets base in the province during the same period, again 1982 to 1988, in which the bank's assets were dropping like crab apples in the fall. Local credit unions saw their assets rise by 22 per cent. Trust companies' assets went up by 30 percent. Incredibly, mortgage companies' assets shot up by 147 per cent, and Alberta Treasury Branches', the Alberta peoples' nationalized bank, its assets skyrocketed by a whopping 167 per cent.
Second, at the same time as the chartered banks business loans in Alberta declined by 50 per cent and their total assets declined by 13 per cent, their total liabilities actually went up by 27 per cent and the value of personal savings held by those banks in Alberta went up by a very healthy 41 per cent. So at precisely the same time that business loans had been declining absolutely and as a percentage of total assets, personal savings have been rising absolutely and as a percentage of total liabilities.
To those familiar with classic capitalist economic theory which holds that banks and such similar financial institutions exist primarily to marshall the savings of
October 17, 1989

individuals in a community and then put those savings to productive use in wealth-creating investment, these diametrically opposite trends must be deeply puzzling, especially during a period in which other locally-based financial institutions, including again, the province's very own nationalized bank, experienced healthy and in some instances, very healthy increases in their assets.
The Minister of Finance, in responding to these facts last June, offered two related explanations. First, he said that it was just a matter of bank business loans reflecting the adjustment in Alberta's economy as it tumbled from the boom-time highs of 1982 to the more sober and appropriate levels of 1988 and second, that it was the fault of the NEP. I will deal with each argument.
To take the second point first, the facts are that the banks, abandonment of their Alberta business assets accelerated after the revoking of the NEP in 1985. Bank business loans in Alberta dropped by 6.2 per cent from 1982 to 1983; by 7.2 per cent from 1983 to 1984; and by 5.4 per cent from 1984 to 1985. Then the NEP was removed. Immediately the banks responded. Business loans dropped like a rock from 1985 to 1986, a plunge of 13 per cent, more than double the previous year's rate of decline. Then from 1986 to 1987, the crash accelerated further, reaching a dizzying 18 per cent drop. Things moderated only slightly from 1987 to 1988 when bank business loans dropped only another 14.4 per cent.
If one wishes to involve the NEP at all, the only reasonable conclusion one can draw from the data is that the NEP, while it was in place, served to moderate the chartered banks' abandonment of Alberta businesses.
The other argument which can be stated, that Alberta has simply been put back in its proper place is, on the face of it, a more reasonable argument. Again, it requires ignoring the record of other locally based financially institutions in the province, but let us for the moment adopt that indulgent ignorance and examine the thesis.
In 1982, the chartered banks had $18.1 billion tied up in business loans in Alberta. That same year, Alberta's GDP at market price was $59.9 billion. By 1988, bank business loans had plummeted to $9.1 billion, for a 50 per cent drop. But Alberta's GDP had risen by almost 20
Adjournment Debate
per cent over the same period up to $63.3 billion. Again, those who advance the thesis that the banks' business loans in Alberta are simply a lock-step puppet of the province's GDP will have to seek support for their thesis from sources other than the available data.
Wait, I hear the cry coming from across the floor. That is not what we said. We said you have to look at Alberta's business loans in light of Alberta's GDP, in light of the national GDP. Got that? Right, Mr. Speaker. Ignore the province's growing savings. Ignore the province's growing GDP. Look instead at what happened to Alberta's GDP as a percentage of the national GDP. Okay, fine. Let us look at what happened.
In 1982, at the same time as Alberta accounted for 14.1 per cent of Canada's GDP, it received 25.3 per cent of the chartered banks' business loans. By 1988, Alberta accounted for only 10.5 per cent of Canada's GDP, a drop of 3.6 per cent. But over the same period, Alberta's share of the banks' business loans dropped to 11.2 per cent, a plunge of 14.1 per cent. Alberta's GDP share drops 3.6 points so its business loans share drops 14.1 points.
Look at it in this way. Express bank business loans as a ratio of GDP. In 1982, that ratio stood at 1 to 2.91; that is, $1 of bank business loans for every $2.91 of GDP. By 1988, that ratio had widened to 1 to 6.93; $1 of bank business loans for every $6.93 of GDP. That is some adjustment over six year.
Again, I would simply ask the government, why did you let it happen? Why did you not do something to staunch this appalling haemorrhage of bank finance capital out of Alberta businesses? While we are at it let me pose as well the following question: Canadians' total personal savings on deposit with Canadian chartered banks rose from $98.9 billion in 1982 to $150.3 billion in 1988, a rise of a little more than 50 per cent. Even expressed in constant 1981 dollars, that is still a rise of 17 per cent, a very healthy trend. Over the same period the total of Canadian chartered banks business loans outstanding in Canada rose all but imperceptibly from $71.6 billion in 1982 to $72.8 billion in 1988. In constant 1981 dollars, that is actually a decline of more than 20 per cent in bank business loans. Again, that is savings up, business loans down.

I would therefore ask the government, is it at all alarmed at this trend which, once again, flies in the face of classic capitalist economics? Having abandoned Alberta businesses to their fate, will the government nonetheless see what it can do to encourage a somewhat less tight-fisted attitude on the part of the banks toward Canadian business in general?
And what the heck, Mr. Speaker, maybe just one more time, the government could explain why it is necessary to exempt Canada's chartered banks from the GST.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it always makes me smile when I see a Member of the New Democratic Party speaking for the corporate sector, when he criticizes them for the rest of the day and in fact the rest of the year. The Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Harvey) pointed out that the bank business loans portfolio in Alberta declined 50 per cent between 1982 and 1988, and his conclusion was that the banks are depriving Albertan businesses of the credit they need to expand.
Mr. Speaker, it is true that the bank business loans portfolio in Alberta declined between 1982 and 1988.
What we must understand is that this decline was not caused by the banks, as the Hon. Member said, "throwing half of their business loans overboard". There were several financial factors that influenced the banks.
I believe the most important factor was that 1982, the first year of the period we are considering, in addition to being a year of transition-the previous years had been years of growth while those that followed immediately afterwards showed a drop in activity-was practically a record year for the resource sector in Canada and especially in Alberta. There are two reasons for this. First, thanks to very high prices in the industry, the resource sector was growing at an unprecedented rate. Second, 1982 was the year when Canadianization of the resource industry was made a priority. As a result of
these two factors, funds borrowed from banks by the resource sector across Canada in 1982 totalled $10.8 billion, which was 14 per cent of total business loans. In 1988, the corresponding figures were, respectively, $5.6 billion and 7 per cent.
Because of the important role played by the resource sector in Alberta's economy, the province's share of total business loans in 1982 rose to 25 per cent, twice the province's share of the GDP. Alberta's share of total business loans in 1988 was 11 per cent, which is closer to its present share of 12 per cent.
The second factor to be considered when we look at bank loans to businesses in Alberta is that the 1980s were a difficult period for the resource sector in Canada, and that understandably, the impact of these problems was particularly severe in Alberta. Because of large loans contracted during the years of rapid growth immediately preceding 1982, many businesses were reorganized, downsized, amalgamated or simply closed down. From 1982 to 1988, non-recovered bank loans in the resource sector, and especially in Alberta, totalled several billion dollars. Following a period of restructuring, the sector has now gained strength.
Another factor we cannot overlook is that many businesses are now resorting to other types of financing. Since 1982, for instance, the use of bank acceptances and securities issues has increased.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I think we can say that the figures submitted by the Hon. Member for Edmonton East are not a reflection of cynical or discriminatory practices. Furthermore, we have every reason to believe that the banks, like other financial institutions, are developing opportunities for business loans as vigorously in Alberta as they are in the rest of the country.
